sources.news_title: Iran and US Hit Tankers in Biggest Wave of Attacks on Shipping Since War Began
sources.text:
Iran and US Hit Tankers in Biggest Wave of Attacks on Shipping Since War Began
Error: Contact form not found.
by Reuters and Algemeiner Staff
Iran said on Wednesday it had attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz after the US sank five Iranian oil tankers, in the biggest declared wave of tit-for-tat attacks on shipping by both sides since the start of the six-month-old war.
The attacks sent the price of oil surging, with benchmark Brent crude futures breaching $100 a barrel for the first time since July. At least one seafarer aboard a tanker was reported killed and another listed as missing.
Iran also said it had fired ballistic missiles at a base used by US forces in Jordan. Attacks by both sides since the end of August have shattered a month of relative calm, with the US and Iran hitting military, shipping and energy assets.
The Revolutionary Guards said they would sharply escalate their response to any further attacks, hitting 20 targets if the enemy struck two or three. Iran would soon release maps of a new, enlarged off-limits zone at sea that would extend as far as Chabahar on the far reaches of Iran‘s coast near Pakistan, the Guards said.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres appealed to all sides to “exercise utmost restraint” and avoid inflaming the already volatile situation in and near the Strait of Hormuz.
Recent days have also seen an escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen, a second theatre of war that threatens global energy supplies from the Middle East.
VIDEO SHOWS IRANIAN TANKERS ABLAZE
The Americans said they destroyed five Iranian oil tankers overnight, releasing video of ships ablaze before they sank. The US military’s Central Command called its attacks a response to Iran‘s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeting a US Navy warship twice with ballistic missiles over the previous two days. No Americans were harmed, the US said.
Washington has announced a new policy of attacking Iranian tankers in retaliation for fire that threatens its warships, and says it has hit 10 so far over the past week.
“Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters during a visit to Colombia.
Iran said it fired on two US ships and eight tankers in response.
One seafarer was killed aboard the oil products tanker Hercules Star while at anchorage off Dubai and another crew member was missing, the vessel’s charterer, Peninsula, said. Maritime security sources said it may have been hit by a drone.
The British maritime security agency UKMTO described a vessel in the vicinity that was listing, possibly taking on water after being struck by a projectile. Reuters could not immediately determine whether this referred to the same ship.
Two Iraqi port officials said a tanker carrying 2 million barrels of fuel oil, the New Andros, had caught fire after being struck by a drone in Iraqi waters. There were no reports of casualties among the 22 crew.
The UKMTO said it had received reports of several merchant ships struck by disabling fire in the northern Gulf and Gulf of Oman, on either side of the strait.
Iran also threatened oil tankers in Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports, according to a statement carried by state media. A maritime security source reported a liquefied natural gas tanker was damaged in the Emirati port of Khor Fakkan.
The IRGC also said on Wednesday it had fired ballistic missiles at a base used by US forces near Al Azraq, in eastern Jordan. Jordan said its air defenses had intercepted 18 of the 20 Iranian missiles, with two falling harmlessly in unpopulated areas. A US official said Iran’s strikes in Jordan were ineffective and all American troops were accounted for.
An explosion was heard in the southern part of the Iranian port city of Jask, coming from the sea, Iran‘s Fars news agency reported late on Wednesday. It said no details were available on the source or cause of the blast.
STRAIT CHOKED OFF
In recent weeks Washington had boasted of increasing success guiding tankers through the strait, which carried a fifth of oil supplies before the war. But any such gradual reopening appears to have been set back by a resumption of fighting this month.
Claudio Galimberti, chief economist at consultancy Rystad Energy, said flows through Hormuz had fallen back as low as 2 million barrels per day, having reached as high as 8 million to 9 million bpd in the week before fighting resumed on Aug. 30.
Even more severe than the rise in crude prices has been a surge in the cost of the fuels refined from it. The politically sensitive average retail price of US diesel hit a fresh all-time high on Wednesday above $5.94 a gallon.
Escalating combat between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned Houthi movement that controls most populated parts of Yemen has created additional uncertainty for energy markets.
On Tuesday, the Houthis launched an attack on four cities in Saudi Arabia, causing huge fires visible from space at oil installations. Saudi authorities said 73 people were wounded.
Saudi authorities announced alerts on Wednesday in two of the cities hit the previous day, but later said the threat had passed.
A Saudi-backed government based in the south of Yemen has launched a multi-pronged assault on areas controlled by the Houthis, who have threatened Saudi shipping in the Red Sea.

sources.news_title: Oil Hits $100 as Iran-U.S. Clash Spreads to Jordan
sources.text:
Brent crude touched $100 a barrel for the first time since July 24 on Wednesday, and the U.S.-Iran conflict crossed into its sharpest week yet after American forces destroyed five more Iranian tankers overnight and Tehran answered with a barrage of missiles at a U.S. base in Jordan. Combined with three tankers disabled or destroyed over the weekend, the toll has reached ten Iranian carriers lost in seven days, a pace that has moved the war from a dispute over declarations about the Strait of Hormuz to one measured directly in ships sunk, missiles intercepted and the price of oil.
U.S. Central Command said its forces struck the five tankers Tuesday night in response to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeting a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles on two separate occasions in two days. Four vessels were hit in the Gulf of Oman and a fifth near Kharg Island, Iran's principal crude export terminal; crews were ordered to abandon ship before the vessels were struck and rendered inoperable, according to the command, which released footage of the operation. Central Command described the ships as part of a multibillion-dollar network funding the Revolutionary Guard and said Iran lacked the means to defend them. The command also rejected an Iranian account claiming that two U.S. warships had been hit, saying no Navy vessel had been struck and that every attempted Revolutionary Guard attack had failed.
Iran's response arrived on multiple fronts before dawn Wednesday. State media said missiles had been launched at U.S. targets in Jordan; Jordan's military said its air defenses intercepted eighteen ballistic missiles, with two others landing in unpopulated areas and no casualties reported. Central Command said it had no information to offer on the strikes inside Jordan. Separately, the Revolutionary Guard's naval branch warned tanker crews docked at ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to leave their vessels immediately, saying the ships could be targeted in retaliation — the first time in this phase of the conflict that Iran has extended a direct threat to shipping already in port rather than in transit. Iran's Sepah News outlet went further Wednesday morning, claiming that naval forces had struck two U.S. vessels and eight oil tankers in the Persian Gulf and inflicted heavy damage while asserting "complete management and control" over the waterway. No independent confirmation of damage to any vessel had surfaced by midday, and no shipping company or flag state had reported being struck.
A separate Iranian claim from Tuesday has drawn a quieter response from Washington. The Revolutionary Guard's naval forces said they had captured an advanced unmanned U.S. submarine near the entrance to the strait, describing a vessel delivered to the fleet in 2025. American officials have not confirmed the claim and have downplayed its significance without explicitly denying that an unmanned craft was lost, leaving open a question that is likely to matter more over the coming months than Wednesday's missile exchanges.
Financial markets moved before officials had finished describing the fighting. Brent for November delivery rose roughly 2.7% to around $100.57 in early trading, its highest level since late July, after touching $99.46 on Tuesday, while West Texas Intermediate climbed above $95. The Dow Jones Industrial Average had already closed Tuesday down more than 500 points as news of the tanker strikes spread. Some financial institutions have warned that sustained attacks on shipping in the Gulf and the Red Sea could push Brent above $120. The escalation lands two days before the release of August producer-price data, which is expected to show wholesale inflation accelerating to 5.4% from 4.7% in July. At the pump, regular gasoline has averaged a record $4.15 a gallon nationwide since Labor Day, and diesel reached a record $5.85 on Friday, up nearly 56% since the war began. President Trump said late Monday that oil prices would drop "precipitously" once the war is won, a forecast the past two days of price movement have not yet borne out.
The fighting has given concrete form to measures Iran previewed earlier in the week. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said Sunday that Tehran would declare a restricted zone stretching from the U.S. blockade line into the Persian Gulf, with any vessel entering it added to Iran's sanctions list, and he described the move Tuesday as a response to American economic pressure, claiming that new missiles had substantially improved Iran's ability to target U.S. warships and bases. Wednesday's Revolutionary Guard statement, describing ships crossing a "prohibited and unsafe zone," suggests Iran is enforcing that exclusion zone in practice before formally declaring it. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday that talks with Oman over a temporary safe corridor for shipping had reached their final stage and would be registered with the International Maritime Organization within days, though no such filing had been reported by Wednesday. President Masoud Pezeshkian said in a social media post that Iran would continue what he called its resistance "until the aggressors are brought to complete regret."
Washington's posture has hardened in step. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking in Colombia on Tuesday, said Iran would keep losing tankers for every attempt to strike a U.S. warship, echoing a ratio Central Command commander Adm. Brad Cooper set out over the weekend — three Iranian tankers destroyed for every two attacks on a U.S. vessel — and one that was applied within hours of two attempted missile attacks. The Treasury Department added a financial dimension the same day, sanctioning 36 entities including every remaining Iranian airline under a campaign the administration calls Operation Economic Outcast, accusing the aviation sector of moving weapons, personnel and illicit cargo and naming service providers in Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Kazakhstan and Malaysia that it said support one of the sanctioned carriers. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that any business done with the airlines risked being cut off from the global financial system. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi responded that after 47 years of sanctions and a war, Washington's answer was simply more of the same.
Traffic through the strait, the measure most relevant to the global economy, has not recovered from last week's collapse. Shipping analytics firm Kpler recorded an average of ten transits a day on Sunday, down from a ten-day average of thirteen on Saturday and more than fifteen on Friday, with most passing vessels using the Iranian-controlled route. Maritime data provider Lloyd's List counted 102 transits for all of last week, against 126 the week before and a prewar baseline of at least 130 ships a day. Rezaei's own figure of seven or eight ships a day, most carrying essential goods into Iran, sits close to those independent counts. The Global Shipping Group, a consortium of eighteen maritime nations including Denmark, the United Kingdom and Canada, said in a rare joint statement Tuesday that the Middle East conflict, alongside the pandemic and the war in Ukraine, represented a structural shift in the operating environment of global trade rather than an isolated shock, and called for stronger adherence to the right of innocent passage under international maritime law.
The parallel conflict on the Red Sea has intensified at a similar pace. A Saudi-led coalition said Houthi strikes on an airport, an air base and oil facilities in southern Saudi Arabia wounded 73 people and forced temporary shutdowns at energy sites; Saudi Arabia retaliated within hours, and Houthi forces reported more than thirty Saudi strikes across several regions by Wednesday. Death tolls from the fighting, most of them among combatants, have been put above 500 since the Iran-aligned movement launched an offensive last week toward the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern entrance to the Red Sea that has become the main route for Saudi crude rerouted around Hormuz. Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan said the Houthis had opened a confrontation they could not sustain while insisting the door to diplomacy remained open. United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, the European Union and the International Committee of the Red Cross each condemned the Houthi strikes or warned of a widening regional war. Rubio said Iran's influence lay behind the attacks and deferred to the fourteen-nation Saudi-led coalition on any response, adding that he did not expect the Pentagon to announce direct American involvement.
The question of wider allied participation moved forward Tuesday. South Korea's defense ministry said it had sent a fact-finding team to assess conditions in the strait, stressing that no troops would be deployed and that the mission did not presuppose an eventual deployment, though the government has said it would consider joining naval operations if its own readiness allowed, with a parliamentary consent motion possible as early as this month. Baghaei has warned that such participation would amount to direct support for the party responsible for the war and would carry serious consequences — a warning that now has a concrete reference point in the Revolutionary Guard's threat to tankers docked in Kuwait and Bahrain, ports through which South Korea sources much of its crude.
Diplomatic movement, such as it is, has shifted toward Beijing. Qatar's foreign ministry said it was working intensively with international partners, including China, to resume dialogue, after Qatar's prime minister met China's foreign minister in Beijing on Monday. China buys roughly 45% of Iran's oil, according to a U.S. government estimate from March, and has rejected American calls to curtail that trade. The outreach follows a week in which Gulf officials have described the American security relationship in conditional terms, with Qatari and Emirati officials each suggesting that geography leaves little alternative to direct engagement with Iran. The nuclear track that formally triggered the war remains stalled: International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi said Monday there was no engagement with Iran, which has said it will not cooperate until a broader political settlement is reached.
Inside Iran, the costs of the war are becoming harder for the government to manage. The price of gasoline for heavy consumers doubled Tuesday to the equivalent of about 7 cents per liter above a monthly quota, the second such increase since December; a 2019 fuel-price increase set off nationwide protests and a crackdown that reportedly killed more than 300 people. Consumption reached a record 145 million liters a day in August against domestic refining capacity of 122 million liters, and the rial traded at a record low of 2.22 million to the dollar on Monday. Iran's state airports company said 27 airports had been damaged in the war's first phase and that radar and navigation systems had been struck again since a ceasefire collapsed in June. In Sistan and Baluchestan province, semi-official media reported that a paramilitary Basij commander was killed Tuesday in what it called a terrorist attack, a reminder that Iran's internal security challenges have continued alongside the war at sea. Bessent said Sunday that Iran still held roughly 30 million barrels of crude that China had not yet purchased.
The human toll has continued to climb on both sides. The Pentagon's casualty tally added 26 wounded in overseas operations Tuesday, the term used for Middle East deployments since July, bringing the total to 403 wounded and at least 18 killed since the war began in February. Iran has confirmed seven personnel killed in the U.S. campaign launched over the Labor Day weekend, and at least five civilians died in a strike on southern Iran that Tehran says hit a wedding — a claim Vice President JD Vance said he was highly skeptical of, though it remains a grievance Iran continues to cite for its expanded retaliation. Two Filipino seafarers were killed aboard a Saudi-flagged tanker in the strait a week ago, and Oman's navy evacuated sixteen of the twenty-five crew members. On Israel's northern front, the military said Monday it would keep operating against threats in southern Lebanon while remaining committed to a ceasefire, after Lebanon's health ministry reported twelve people killed in strikes, most in a residential building. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said the strikes undermined efforts to prevent a wider regional escalation.
What separates this week from earlier flashpoints in the conflict is that both sides' stated rules are now being carried out rather than merely announced. Washington has a published exchange rate for tankers and warships and has applied it twice within four days. Tehran is enforcing an exclusion zone by missile and by claim before any formal document exists, pursuing a shipping corridor it says is close to registration, and testing a threat to tankers in allied ports that has not yet resulted in an attack. Each side's account of Wednesday's fighting — an Iranian claim of damage to U.S. warships that Washington calls false, and a Central Command insistence that its own vessels came through untouched — will be measured against insurance filings, port logs and satellite imagery in the days ahead. Until then, the only figures not in dispute are the ones that moved Wednesday morning: ten Iranian tankers destroyed in a week, twenty missiles fired at Jordan, and Brent crude above $100 a barrel for the first time in more than six weeks.

sources.news_title: Oil prices top $101 a barrel as U.S.-Iran tanker war escalates
sources.text:
Crude oil prices surged past $101 a barrel on Wednesday as conflict between the United States and Iran spread across the Persian Gulf, stoking fears of prolonged disruptions to energy exports through the Strait of Hormuz.
Brent crude crossed $101 for the first time since July after the U.S. destroyed five Iranian tankers on Tuesday
Brent futures were trading at $101.25 a barrel, a gain of 3.4%, as of 11:12 a.m. ET — a threshold the international benchmark had not reached since July. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures were up 3.6%, changing hands at $96.38 a barrel.
The U.S. military destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers on Tuesday in response to attempted attacks on an American warship, U.S. Central Command said. No American personnel were harmed. Four of the tankers were struck in the Gulf of Oman and one near Kharg Island, a critical hub for Iran's oil exports in the Persian Gulf, according to CNN.
Oil prices also got a boost earlier Tuesday after Iran-backed Houthi rebels attacked Saudi oil and other infrastructure, according to CNN. Saudi-led forces said dozens of civilians were injured and vowed to respond. The Houthis have separately targeted the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a waterway connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, adding further pressure on regional energy flows.
The two countries had largely held back from direct military engagement for roughly a month after hostilities spiked in July, during which time Washington leaned on sanctions and other economic tools to press Tehran. Hostilities have since flared again, with Iran continuing to threaten commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz as the conflict enters its seventh month.
Brent and U.S. crude are each up more than 60% this year. That has driven retail fuel prices higher: the national average for gasoline reached $4.22 per gallon on Wednesday, while diesel hit a record $5.94 per gallon, according to AAA data cited by CNN. Wednesday's per-gallon gasoline price jumped by 7.3 cents, marking the steepest daily climb recorded since May 1, AAA data showed.
The broader market felt the strain. The S&P 500 extended Tuesday's 0.6% decline with a further 0.3% drop Wednesday, while the 10-year Treasury yield hovered at 4.8%, approaching levels not seen since 2023.
Speaking on CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia," Goldman Sachs $GS co-head of global commodities research Daan Struyven warned that the latest flare-up has meaningfully increased the probability of oil prices breaching $120 a barrel, particularly if tanker strikes keep Persian Gulf export volumes depressed. Goldman's central scenario envisions Persian Gulf shipments eventually rebounding as producers work around the disruptions — including by redirecting cargoes and expanding overland pipeline options, Struyven said.

sources.news_title: Iran War Escalates as U.S. and Tehran Clash Over Strait of Hormuz, Tankers and Regional Bases
sources.text:
|                            Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...                        | 
Iran War Escalates as U.S. and Tehran Clash Over Strait of Hormuz, Tankers and Regional Bases
The war between the United States and Iran has entered one of its most dangerous phases in recent days, with fighting escalating around the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian oil tankers being destroyed by U.S. forces, Iranian missile attacks against U.S. positions and a widening campaign by Iran-backed forces against American allies.
The latest escalation began with a series of attacks on U.S. naval forces and commercial shipping and has rapidly developed into a broader confrontation over control of the strategic waterway. The New York Times reported Wednesday that Iran is signaling a willingness to escalate its fight with the United States as its economic situation deteriorates and Tehran becomes increasingly concerned that its ability to control or influence the Strait of Hormuz is slipping.
The events of the past three days have effectively turned the Strait of Hormuz into the central battlefield of the war.
U.S. Destroys Five Iranian Oil Tankers
The most significant U.S. military action came Tuesday, when U.S. forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps attempted to strike a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles.
According to the Associated Press, the five vessels were identified as the Kivik, Charminar, Horizon 1, Riesco and Derya. American officials said the tanker crews were instructed to abandon their ships before the strikes. No American casualties were reported.
U.S. Central Command said the attacks were carried out after the IRGC attempted to target an American warship twice over a two-day period. CENTCOM said the warship successfully evaded the missiles.
The U.S. military has portrayed the tanker strikes as a defensive response to Iranian attacks and as part of its effort to enforce a blockade and restrict Iranian oil shipments.
The strikes represented a major expansion of the maritime campaign. Earlier in the week, U.S. forces had already struck three Iranian oil tankers, including a vessel near Kharg Island, one of Iran’s most important oil-export facilities.
Iran Retaliates With Missile Attacks
Iran quickly threatened retaliation.
On Tuesday night and into Wednesday, Iranian forces launched ballistic missiles toward the U.S. military presence at Al-Azraq in Jordan. Jordan’s military said it intercepted 18 of 20 missiles, with the remaining missiles falling in unpopulated areas. No casualties were reported.
The attack demonstrated that Tehran was prepared to expand its response beyond the immediate maritime confrontation.
Iran has repeatedly warned that U.S. military installations throughout the Middle East could become targets if Washington continues attacking Iranian shipping.
The New York Times reported that Iranian leaders have adopted an increasingly aggressive posture because the U.S. blockade and other economic pressure are threatening one of Tehran’s most important sources of revenue: oil exports. Analysts cited by the newspaper said Iran increasingly sees escalation as one of its few remaining forms of leverage against Washington.
Iran Claims Attacks on 10 Ships
The confrontation escalated again Wednesday.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard claimed its naval forces attacked two U.S. vessels and eight oil tankers in the Persian Gulf. Iranian authorities also said their forces targeted additional ships attempting to enter what Tehran described as a restricted and unsafe area around the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran did not publicly identify the U.S. vessels or provide independent evidence confirming the extent of the damage.
The United States, meanwhile, disputed Iranian claims that American warships had been successfully hit.
Reuters described the exchange as the biggest declared wave of reciprocal attacks on shipping since the war began. The news agency reported that at least one seafarer had been killed and another was missing amid the latest maritime attacks.
The British maritime security organization UKMTO also reported multiple vessels being hit by disabling fire in the northern Gulf and Gulf of Oman.
The result has been a dramatic reduction in commercial traffic through the waterway.
Strait of Hormuz Becomes the Center of the War
The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most important energy chokepoints. The waterway connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea and normally carries a substantial portion of the world’s seaborne oil and liquefied natural gas.
The conflict has sharply reduced traffic.
Reuters reported Wednesday that oil exports from the Gulf remain substantially below prewar levels despite some vessels continuing to move through the region using increasingly risky methods. Some tankers are reportedly shutting off their tracking systems to reduce the possibility of being targeted.
Reuters estimated that Gulf oil exports are running at roughly two-thirds of prewar levels, while other market-data providers have reported substantially lower flows. The uncertainty itself has become a major problem for energy markets because traders cannot reliably determine how much oil is actually moving through Hormuz.
Iran has also threatened to establish a new exclusion zone around the waterway.
Tehran says the measure would prevent ships from entering areas it considers dangerous. Washington has rejected Iranian claims that American vessels have violated Iranian restrictions and has continued efforts to keep shipping routes open.
U.S. Blockade Puts Pressure on Tehran
The maritime confrontation is not simply about individual ships.
It is also a struggle over Iran’s ability to export oil and generate the revenue needed to sustain its government and military.
The New York Times reported that the U.S. blockade has made it increasingly difficult for Iran to ship oil, placing additional pressure on an economy already damaged by the war and sanctions. The newspaper said Iranian officials are increasingly worried that their grip on the Strait of Hormuz is weakening.
That creates a dangerous strategic calculation for Tehran.
Backing down could mean accepting greater U.S. control over the maritime environment and further restrictions on Iranian oil exports. Escalating, however, creates the possibility of an even wider American military response.
Iran appears to be choosing escalation.
Houthis Open Another Front Against Saudi Arabia
The conflict has also spread deeper into the Arabian Peninsula.
Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen launched attacks against four Saudi cities Tuesday, injuring 73 people and setting oil-related facilities ablaze, according to Reuters.
The attacks mark a significant expansion of the regional conflict because Saudi Arabia is a major U.S. partner and one of the world’s largest oil producers.
The Houthis have also threatened shipping through the Red Sea, potentially creating a second major disruption to global maritime commerce.
The Associated Press reported that Saudi-backed forces subsequently carried out dozens of airstrikes against Houthi positions in Yemen. The renewed fighting threatens a fragile four-year truce and could turn Yemen back into another major battlefield connected to the wider U.S.-Iran confrontation.
The AP also reported that Houthi attacks on Saudi energy facilities temporarily disrupted operations.
That means the war is now threatening both major maritime routes connecting Middle Eastern oil to world markets — the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.
Oil Surges Above $100
The latest fighting immediately hit global energy markets.
Brent crude rose above $100 per barrel Wednesday, reaching its highest level since July. Reuters reported that Brent climbed more than 2.8% in early trading as investors reacted to the latest U.S.-Iran attacks and the threat of additional supply disruptions.
The Financial Times reported Brent reached approximately $101.55, while the conflict has reduced traffic through Hormuz dramatically.
The consequences are already being felt by American consumers.
According to the Associated Press, U.S. gasoline prices have climbed to about $4.22 per gallon, while diesel reached approximately $5.94 per gallon, adding further inflationary pressure to an economy already dealing with elevated prices.
The energy shock also presents a problem for the Federal Reserve. Higher fuel and transportation costs can feed inflation, potentially complicating decisions over interest rates.
Markets React to the Escalation
Wall Street also reacted negatively Wednesday.
The AP reported that the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell more than 400 points, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq also declined as investors assessed the possibility of a prolonged energy shock. Oil companies were among the few major sectors benefiting from higher crude prices.
Reuters reported that European and global markets also weakened, while bond yields increased as investors worried that higher energy prices could keep inflation elevated and force central banks to maintain tighter monetary policies.
The economic consequences could become much more severe if the fighting further restricts oil shipments.
Bank of America analysts have warned that crude prices could potentially reach as high as $150 per barrel if major energy infrastructure is damaged, according to the AP.
A Dangerous New Phase of the War
The events of September 7 through September 9 have fundamentally changed the character of the conflict.
What had already been a prolonged U.S.-Iran war has increasingly become a battle over maritime control, oil exports and access to the Strait of Hormuz.
The United States is attempting to prevent Iran from using the waterway and its oil fleet to finance the war while maintaining pressure on Tehran’s military infrastructure.
Iran, meanwhile, is demonstrating that it still has the ability to threaten U.S. forces, attack commercial shipping and mobilize allied forces across the region.
The confrontation now extends from Iranian waters to Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and international shipping lanes, creating multiple opportunities for further escalation.
The New York Times reported that Iranian leaders appear increasingly willing to take greater risks precisely because their economic and strategic position is deteriorating.
That dynamic makes the coming days particularly dangerous.
Neither side appears prepared to concede control of the maritime battlefield, while every new attack creates pressure for retaliation. With commercial shipping already severely disrupted and oil prices again above $100 a barrel, the consequences of the Iran war are no longer confined to the Middle East.
The immediate question is whether the latest exchange remains a contained battle over Hormuz — or becomes the beginning of a much wider regional war involving U.S. forces, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and other American allies.

sources.news_title: US Forces Destroy 10 Iranian Tankers Linked to Shadow Network in Past Week: CENTCOM
sources.text:
American forces have destroyed 10 Iranian tankers with ties to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) over the past week, according to the U.S. military.
The attacks on Iranian tankers were carried out in response to attempted Iranian strikes against U.S. Navy warships in the Middle East.
In a Sept. 9 statement on social media, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) denied claims made by the IRGC that Iranian attacks successfully struck U.S. warships.
Iranian military spokesman Ebrahim Zolfaghari said on Wednesday that Iran had targeted two U.S. warships. The Iranian state-run Fars News Agency claimed that the two vessels were damaged by ballistic missiles.
The IRGC also said it attacked eight oil tankers that were trying to cross a “prohibited and unsafe” area in the Strait of Hormuz.
“[IRGC] forces have claimed they struck two U.S. Navy destroyers operating in the Middle East. This is completely false,” CENTCOM said, responding to the claim in a statement on X.
CENTCOM confirmed on Wednesday that no U.S. warships had been hit by Iranian strikes and that all of the IRGC’s attempted attacks on them had failed.
The command added that U.S. forces had successfully destroyed 10 Iranian tankers over the past week.
CENTCOM said the tankers were “part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC” and suggested that Iran could not defend the ships.
The Trump administration has warned that the United States will strike Iranian tankers if the regime continues attacking U.S. Navy warships.
“Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday.
The U.S. military has continued to enforce a blockade on maritime trade with Iran since July 14.
President Donald Trump ordered U.S. forces to restart the blockade following the collapse of a memorandum of understanding between the United States and Iran that had temporarily paused the conflict and outlined a peace plan.
As of Sept. 7, U.S. forces had redirected 94 commercial vessels, disabled three ships, and boarded two others to ensure compliance with the U.S. naval blockade, according to CENTCOM.
On Sept. 8, U.S. forces destroyed the IRGC crude oil carriers Kaviz, Charminar, Horizon 1, and Riesco in the Gulf of Oman. The U.S. military also destroyed the Derya near Kharg Island.
The Iranian crude oil carriers were part of the shadow network accused of funding the IRGC and its proxy groups in the Middle East, CENTCOM said.
The strikes against Iranian oil tankers were carried out after the IRGC attempted to attack a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice in two days.
U.S. forces also struck three Iranian crude oil carriers on Sept. 5 after the IRGC launched ballistic missiles at two U.S. Navy warships.
CENTCOM confirmed that a U.S. aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer evaded the Iranian attacks and that no Americans were injured.
The U.S. retaliatory strikes permanently disabled the IRGC crude oil carriers Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and Stark 1 near Jask. U.S. forces also destroyed the Kylo in the Gulf of Oman.
The three Iranian crude oil tankers targeted in the Sept. 5 strikes were also part of a “multibillion-dollar shadow network” funding the IRGC and Tehran’s regional proxy groups, CENTCOM said.
“Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost—taking out three of yours,” Adm. Brad Cooper, CENTCOM commander, said in a statement following the strikes.
The Epoch Times reached out to CENTCOM for further comment but did not receive a response before publication time.

sources.news_title: Tanker War Erupts in the Gulf as US and Iran Trade Blows Around Hormuz
sources.text:
The United States struck five Iranian crude oil carriers on Sept. 8 after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles, according to U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM). The strikes followed attacks on three Iranian oil tankers on Sept. 5, bringing the number of Iranian tankers hit by U.S. forces to eight in four days.
The attacks have added a new dimension to the conflict around the Strait of Hormuz, a critical energy chokepoint between Iran and Oman. Before the war, oil flows through the strait averaged about 20 million barrels per day, equivalent to roughly 20% of global petroleum liquids consumption.
The U.S. Energy Information Administration estimated that only 4.9 million barrels per day of crude oil and petroleum liquids moved through Hormuz in the second quarter of 2026, compared with 21.6 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter of 2025.
US Strikes Eight Iranian Tankers in Four Days
On Sept. 8, CENTCOM said its forces destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers, such as M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1 and M/T Riesco in the Gulf of Oman, and M/T Derya near Kharg Island.
According to CENTCOM, the attacks followed two attempted ballistic-missile attacks by the IRGC against a U.S. Navy warship over two days.
The American vessel evaded the attacks and continued operating in regional waters, and no U.S. personnel were injured, CENTCOM said. American forces directed the tanker crews to abandon their vessels before the ships were struck and rendered inoperable.
On Sept. 5, CENTCOM said its forces struck three additional Iranian crude oil carriers after the IRGC launched ballistic missiles toward a U.S. aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer.
CENTCOM said it permanently disabled M/T Downy off Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask. It also destroyed the unladen M/T Kylo, also known as the Noxen, in the Gulf of Oman after the crew was ordered to abandon the vessel.
"The three Iranian crude oil tankers are part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies," CENTCOM said. "Iran has no means by which to defend them."
CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper spelt out the formula Washington is applying, "If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost - taking out three of yours. We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet."
The Sept. 5 and Sept. 8 strikes show that tanker attacks have become part of the U.S.-Iran military confrontation, with Washington linking strikes on Iranian oil carriers to attempted attacks on American naval forces.
Iran's Retaliation: Jordan Base, Warships and Commercial Tankers
Iran has said it retaliated after the latest U.S. strikes. The IRGC confirmed that five tankers were targeted and said it launched missile attacks against the Al-Azraq air base in Jordan, claiming hangars used by U.S. fighter jets were destroyed. It also claimed ballistic-missile attacks on U.S. Navy destroyers DDG-119 and DDG-53, alleging significant damage.
Jordan has separately reported repeated Iranian missile attacks during the conflict. Jordanian authorities have said its air defenses intercepted Iranian missiles aimed at the country.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they struck two American vessels and eight oil tankers in the Gulf, framing the attacks as retaliation for the U.S. strikes on five Iranian tankers. The IRGC also warned crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels, saying the ships could be targeted.
Iran's Foreign Ministry condemned the tanker strikes as an illegal act of aggression. "The aggressive actions by the United States against Iranian commercial vessels not only represent a dangerous escalation of tensions in the region but also constitute an outright threat to regional and international peace and security," the Iranian Foreign Ministry said.
Tehran Signals Further Escalation
Iranian officials have also signaled that Tehran does not intend to limit its response to previous patterns.
Iran's chief negotiator and parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf ruled out any return to measured responses. "The era of 'proportionate responses' is over," Ghalibaf said in a speech posted to Telegram on Sept. 6. "The rules of the game have changed, and from now on, any transgression against the interests and security of Iran will receive a 'faster, heavier, and more painful' response."
Iranian lawmaker and parliamentary security spokesman Hassan Ghashghavi described the attacks on US warships as part of "an existential war with America," arguing that Washington's naval blockade "should never have existed" in the first place.
The statements indicate that Tehran is presenting the latest attacks as part of a broader confrontation rather than isolated retaliatory strikes.
Background: Months of Fighting Around Hormuz
The current escalation follows months of disruption around the Strait of Hormuz.
Military operations started Feb. 28, and the strait was effectively closed to normal commercial traffic. The United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June with the goal of stopping the conflict and opening up the waterway. EIA said tanker traffic subsequently increased, but renewed attacks later reduced shipments again.
EIA projected oil flows through Hormuz at 21.6 million bpd in the fourth quarter of 2025, prior to the conflict, but decreased to 4.9 million bpd in the second quarter of 2026. The disruption has helped to make the oil price more expensive and volatile, it said.
The waterway is especially significant due to the limited capacity of alternative waterways. EIA believes that pipelines in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Iran could divert only a portion of the oil normally passing through Hormuz.
The conflict has therefore affected not only military operations but also global energy markets. EIA reported that Brent crude reached as high as $105 per barrel on July 23 after renewed attacks on tankers and reduced shipments through Hormuz.
The latest tanker strikes have increased the risks surrounding commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz. The immediate focus will be on whether Iran carries out further attacks against U.S. naval forces or commercial shipping and whether the United States expands strikes against Iranian oil and military assets.
The key issue is whether tanker traffic through Hormuz can recover. EIA's latest assessment says flows remained severely constrained through August, with a gradual recovery expected in September, although it expects some regional oil-production disruptions to continue into 2027.

sources.news_title: Donald Trump Just Ordered US Military Forces to Sink Iran’s Tanker Fleet and Tehran Is Already Firing Back
sources.text:
There was much more activity overnight in the war in Iran, as the U.S.S, reacting to what they claimed was an attempt to attack one of their warships, struck five Iranian oil tankers. After that, Iran retaliated by firing missiles at Jordan.
U.S. Central Command issued a statement about the exchanges of fire, which included video of one of the tanker explosions. CENTCOM stated that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a Naval warship with ballistic missiles twice in two days, although neither ship was struck, and no American personnel were harmed.
CENTCOM, as a result, “destroyed the IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1, and M/T Riesco in the Gulf of Oman as well as M/T Derya near Kharg Island,” the statement said.
“All IRGC attempts against U.S. Navy warships have failed,” CENTCOM added.
According to the New York Times, the IRGC “vowed to retaliate” and warned tankers near Kuwait and Bahrain to evacuate. Soon after that, the Guards said they had fired on two U.S. destroyers and also launched a “heavy missile strike” at Jordan.
Jordan’s military, in turn, said in a statement, per the Times, that of the Iranian ballistic missiles, 18 had been intercepted, while two more fell in unpopulated areas.
Ship For a Ship
Last week, CENTCOM’s commander, Adm. Brad Cooper, had warned the Iranians.
“Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost —taking out three of yours,” the Admiral said in a statement by CENTCOM. “We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.”
The exchanges of fire follow what looked two weeks ago like a pivot on the part of the Trump administration towards sanctions and economic pressure, especially considering the upcoming midterm elections as well as reports about dwindling munitions stockpiles.
But now, it appears, military escalation is back on.
“A Willingness to Escalate”
A separate New York Times analysis, published Wednesday, looked at what the newspaper calls “an increasingly aggressive approach” on the part of the Iranians. One example? This week’s attempted attack on a U.S. naval warship, a first during the war.
Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, told the Times that the attack on the ships represented a major escalation.
“Both sides are trying to dictate their red lines and trying to push the red lines of the other side as far back as they can,” Azizi told the newspaper.
He added that just as Iran has improved its capabilities throughout the war when it comes to attacking military bases with precision, they may have developed a similar capability when it comes to hitting warships.
Iran, the Times said, “faces mounting economic pressure, and they worry that their grip on the Strait of Hormuz is slipping,” as the American blockade has made it more difficult for them to ship oil.
And Iranian leaders have been talking tougher.
Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, the Iranian parliament speaker, told lawmakers over the weekend that the time for “proportionate responses” on Iran’s part was over. Security chief Mohsen Rezaei also announced plans to create a “restricted zone” in the Persian Gulf.
“How do you regain the momentum? You escalate,” said Farzan Sabet, an Iran analyst at the Geneva Graduate Institute, told the Times of Iran’s current predicament. Sabet expected Iran to up the pressure without necessarily restarting the war.
“All signs point to a make-or-break moment,” Mohammad Ali Shabani, an Iran analyst and editor of a regional news website, told the newspaper.
“I’m not sure the Iranians are going to wait until after the elections to be attacked if diplomacy fails.”
In the meantime, Iran’s allies in Yemen, the Houthis, launched a major attack this week on Saudi Arabia’s oil infrastructure, which led the price of oil to rise over $100 a barrel for the first time since July.
“The ongoing crisis in the Middle East has diminished hopes of U.S.-Iran talks and a return to normal oil flows soon,” OilPrice.com said.
About the Author: Stephen Silver
Stephen Silver is an award-winning journalist, essayist, and film critic, and contributor to the Philadelphia Inquirer, the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, Broad Street Review, and Splice Today. The co-founder of the Philadelphia Film Critics Circle, Stephen lives in suburban Philadelphia with his wife and two sons. For over a decade, Stephen has authored thousands of articles that focus on politics, national security, technology, and the economy. sources.news_title: Oil Tops $100 For First Time Since July As US Destroys Five Iranian Tankers
sources.text:
Oil prices topped $100 per barrel Wednesday for the first time since July after American forces destroyed five Iranian tankers.
Brent crude rose 2.7% to $100.57 a barrel Wednesday morning, and last crossed $100 on July 24, according to ABC News. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) rose 2% to about $95 a barrel.
The national average price of regular gasoline rose to $4.22 a gallon Wednesday from $2.98 two days before the Iran war began Feb. 28, according to American Automobile Association (AAA) data.
U.S. Central Command said its forces destroyed four Iranian crude carriers in the Gulf of Oman and a fifth near Kharg Island on Tuesday after Iran fired ballistic missiles at a U.S. Navy warship twice in two days. The command said Wednesday that U.S. forces destroyed 10 Iranian tankers in the past week. The vessels were part of a “multibillion-dollar shadow network” that funds the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) said.
Iran fired 20 ballistic missiles toward Jordan overnight, the Jordan Armed Forces said Wednesday. Jordanian air defenses destroyed 18 of them and two fell in unpopulated areas. The military recorded no casualties.
Iranian state-aligned media claimed the IRGC struck two U.S. Navy destroyers. CENTCOM, in a Wednesday morning X post, called the claim “completely FALSE” and said no U.S. warship has been hit.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry said Wednesday that its strikes on U.S. targets in Jordan were “defensive” and called the tanker attacks “a dangerous escalation of tensions in the region,” according to ABC News.
🚫 CLAIM: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) forces have claimed they struck two U.S. Navy destroyers operating in the Middle East. This is completely FALSE.
✅ FACT: No U.S. Navy warship has been struck; all IRGC attempted attacks failed. Meanwhile, U.S. forces… pic.twitter.com/yfC4OcwZ1f
Iran-backed Houthi rebels attacked southwestern Saudi Arabia early Tuesday, wounding at least 73 people and striking oil infrastructure, according to CNN. Saudi Arabia has routed most of its crude exports through the Red Sea port of Yanbu since Iran effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz, CNN reported. (RELATED: Saudi Arabia Vows Retaliation After Iran-Backed Houthis Attack Oil Facilities)
Ship traffic through the strait has fallen to its lowest level since May, according to Fox News. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, the country’s top negotiator, wrote on X Monday that American oil and gas facilities in the region are “sprawling, accessible, and exposed,” Reuters reported.
Iran raised the gasoline price for its heaviest users Tuesday, its second such increase since December, according to The Associated Press. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News that China has “probably only about 30 million barrels” of Iranian crude left to buy.
The national average diesel price hit a record $5.94 a gallon Wednesday, according to AAA data.

sources.news_title: Iran's Aggression Towards US Forces Results in Major Setbacks
sources.text:
Iran’s recent efforts to attack U.S. military forces have not only missed their targets but have also provoked a powerful counteraction from the United States. As tensions escalate, the U.S. has ramped up its operations against Iranian oil tankers associated with the Islamic Revolution.
These strikes have resulted in significant losses for Iran, highlighting the impotence of their military strategy. The ongoing conflict serves as a stark reminder of the risks involved when challenging American military might.
Failed Attacks and U.S. Response
The Iranian regime’s failed assaults underscore their inability to effectively project power. Each unsuccessful attempt has led to further retaliation from the U.S. military, showcasing a clear disparity in capability.
The destruction of these oil tankers not only hampers Iranian funding but also sends a strong message against their aggressive tactics.

sources.text:
The U.S. military said it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday in response to the latest attacks on its warships and Tehran hit back at American targets in Jordan, the latest burst of back-and-forth strikes that have lurched the sides back toward open hostilities in a more than 6-month-old war. Following the latest American strikes, Iran launched missiles toward U.S. targets in Jordan, Iranian state-run media said. U.S. Central Command said it had no information to offer about the strikes on the Jordanian airbase.
The latest strikes are part of a dual economic and military approach by President Donald Trump as he struggles to bring an end to the war. The Trump administration on Tuesday also imposed sanctions on additional elements of Iran’s aviation industry, targeting more than two dozen commercial and private airlines as well as foreign cargo service providers, in its new push to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners. Both the U.S. and Iran are seeking to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz, where about one-fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war began. sources.news_title: US Destroys Five Iranian Tankers as Iran Fires Missiles at Jordan, Oil Tops $100
sources.text:
Fighting between the United States and Iran intensified sharply on Tuesday night, with U.S. forces destroying five Iranian oil tankers and Iran retaliating by striking civilian vessels in the Persian Gulf and firing missiles at U.S. forces based in Jordan. Global oil prices climbed above $100 a barrel for the first time since July as the escalation rattled markets.
U.S. Central Command said the tankers were destroyed by American airstrikes after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched ballistic missiles at a U.S. Navy warship on two separate occasions within two days.
“The U.S. warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed,” CENTCOM said.
CENTCOM identified the vessels destroyed in the Gulf of Oman as the M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1 and M/T Riesco, along with the M/T Derya near Kharg Island. The military said crews were ordered to abandon ship before the strikes.
Those five tankers, combined with three others struck on September 5, bring the total destroyed in the past week to ten. CENTCOM described the vessels as part of a “multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies,” adding that “Iran has no means by which to defend these vessels.”
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking during a trip to Colombia on Tuesday, warned that the strikes would continue. “Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” he said.
Iran Claims Retaliatory Strikes
The IRGC claimed it struck at least ten ships near the Strait of Hormuz in response. The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations center said it had received unconfirmed reports of several merchant ships in the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman hit by “disabling fire,” including one vessel off the coast of the United Arab Emirates reported to be listing and possibly taking on water.
Iraqi officials said a Panama-flagged tanker, the New Andros, was struck by a drone in Iraqi territorial waters and caught fire. Iraqi rescue boats extinguished the blaze, and no casualties were reported.
Iranian state media published a statement from the IRGC warning oil tanker crews near the ports of Kuwait and Bahrain to evacuate their vessels immediately, accusing the two countries of hosting American forces and being “complicit in their actions.”
The IRGC also claimed it struck two U.S. warships in addition to eight tankers and ten other vessels it described as “non-compliant” in waters it claims to control. CENTCOM rejected that claim outright, calling it “completely false.”
“No U.S. Navy warship has been struck; all IRGC attempted attacks failed. Meanwhile, U.S. forces have successfully destroyed 10 Iranian tankers in just the last week,” CENTCOM said.
Missiles Fired at Jordan Intercepted
Iran also launched twenty ballistic missiles at Jordan, which hosts an American military base and is a key U.S. ally in the region. Iranian state media claimed the strike caused “heavy damage,” but Jordanian and American officials said the attack caused no casualties or damage.
The Jordanian military said its air defense systems intercepted 18 of the 20 missiles, with the remaining two landing in unpopulated areas. U.S. officials called the Iranian attack “ineffective” and said all American personnel in Jordan were accounted for.
Oil Markets React
Brent crude, the global benchmark, rose above $100 per barrel in trading Wednesday as the conflict escalated, though it remains below the $126-per-barrel peak reached since the war began at the end of February.
PVM analyst Tamas Varga said the price surge reflects investor concern that shipping through the Strait of Hormuz will remain disrupted. “Oil investors are expressing their view about the impact of the latest bout of escalation in the Middle East in an unambiguous way. They are voting with their dollar, and this vote strongly indicates that unless the Strait of Hormuz re-opens, and oil starts flowing again uninterruptedly, supply will not be aligned with demand in the foreseeable future,” Varga said.

sources.text:
The U.S. has rejected claims by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard that it struck two American vessels in retaliation for recent U.S. attacks on Iranian tankers. U.S. Central Command said no Navy warship had been hit and that all Iranian attempts failed.
According to CENTCOM, U.S. forces have destroyed 10 Iranian tankers over the past week. Washington says the vessels were linked to a shadow network allegedly financing the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Iran also claimed it captured a U.S. unmanned underwater vehicle. However, the U.S. Navy said the drone malfunctioned, was an older model and carried no sensitive information. The episode highlights the growing role of autonomous military technology in U.S. operations across the region.

sources.news_title: U.S. forces strike five Iranian oil tankers, U.S. Central Command says
U.S. forces decimate Iran’s illegal “shadow fleet”, destroy 10...
sources.text:
The U.S. military says it has destroyed a total of 10 Iranian oil tankers over the past few weeks, a staggering blow to the radical Islamic country’s illegal “shadow fleet” that brings in billions to Tehran every year.
The updated total was released Wednesday as U.S. and Iranian forces traded fresh strikes.
U.S. Central Command disclosed the updated total of destroyed shadow fleet tankers while denying a separate Iranian claim that its forces had struck two U.S. Navy destroyers.
“The IRGC claim of a successful strike is completely FALSE,” CENTCOM said in a post on X. “No U.S. Navy warship has been struck; all IRGC attempted attacks failed. Meanwhile, U.S. forces have successfully destroyed 10 Iranian tankers in just the last week. These vessels were part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC, and Iran cannot defend them.”
🚫 CLAIM: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) forces have claimed they struck two U.S. Navy destroyers operating in the Middle East. This is completely FALSE.
✅ FACT: No U.S. Navy warship has been struck; all IRGC attempted attacks failed. Meanwhile, U.S. forces… pic.twitter.com/yfC4OcwZ1f
— U.S. Central Command (@CENTCOM) September 9, 2026
The destroyed oil tanker ships came in a string of blows from U.S. forces. On Sept. 5, U.S. forces destroyed three Iranian oil carriers, the M/T Downy, M/T Stark 1, and M/T Kylo, after the IRGC launched ballistic missiles at two U.S. Navy warships that evaded the attacks unharmed.
Three days later, on Sept. 8, U.S. forces destroyed five more tankers, the M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1, M/T Riesco, and M/T Derya, after Iran twice targeted a U.S. warship with ballistic missiles over a two-day span. In each case, CENTCOM said American forces ordered the tankers’ crews to abandon ship before striking the vessels.
The remaining two tankers destroyed by U.S. forces have not yet been made public.
The fighting has spread beyond the “shadow fleet” and American Navy in the Gulf. Iran fired missiles toward U.S. targets in Jordan following the Sept. 8 strikes, according to Iranian state media. Jordan’s military said its air defenses intercepted all the missiles, allowing two others to land in unpopulated areas, and reported no casualties. Jordan hosts American forces and has increasingly found targeted by Iranian missiles.
Iran also claimed a smaller symbolic win, saying its navy seized a U.S. Navy underwater drone near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz.
U.S. military spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins downplayed the incident, and said the drone had malfunctioned more than a day earlier while conducting surveillance and was already dead in the water when it was scooped up.
“It was in a commercially available configuration so we aren’t concerned,” Hawkins said. He said it was an older, defective model that carried no classified sonar, radar equipment, or sensitive data.
The war between the U.S., Israel, and Iran, now well into its seventh month, shows no sign of slowing, with strikes by Iranian forces and their allies now reaching Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, and other U.S. allies.

sources.news_title: Tehran Targets U.S. Base in Jordan In Retaliation for U.S. Destroying Iranian Oil Tankers
sources.text:
Oil prices soared above $100 a barrel again Wednesday for the first time since July as the U.S. and Iran exchanged tit-for-tat strikes amid renewed hostilities.
Iran targeted a U.S. base in Jordan with a series of missiles overnight, framing the assault as "retaliation for" the U.S. military destroying five Iranian oil tankers.
A spokesperson for the Jordanian Armed Forces said a barrage of “20 ballistic missiles” had been launched towards its territory in the early hours. Jordan's air defense system successfully intercepted and destroyed 18 of the missiles, while the remaining two "fell in areas devoid of population centers."
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on Wednesday, in a statement carried by state media, said it had also attacked two U.S. vessels, eight oil tankers, and 10 “noncompliant vessels” near the Strait of Hormuz, as tensions simmer over the maritime chokepoint.
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) denied the IRGC’s claims regarding the U.S. vessels, insisting that “no U.S. Navy warship has been struck” as “all IRGC attempted attacks failed.”
CENTCOM said its operation against the five Iranian crude oil tankers on Tuesday was in response to the IRGC targeting a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles earlier in the week. "The U.S. warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed,” said CENTCOM.
The attacks on shipping mark a serious escalation of the war, which experienced a brief respite before flaring up again last week. The strikes are unfolding as President Donald Trump pursues a campaign of military and economic pressure on Tehran, with Iranian officials threatening it could escalate the conflict further by targeting U.S. oil and gas interests in the Gulf.
Oil rises as Middle East turmoil intensifies
Brent crude oil prices soared to $101.58 a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since July, deepening concerns over global supply.
The impact is already being felt across energy markets, with the average retail price of U.S. diesel hitting an all-time high of $5.94 on Wednesday, according to the American Automobile Association.
The continued conflict has also taken a toll on U.S. strategic petroleum reserves, which currently stand at their lowest levels since 1982.
The flare-up of the Iran war, now in its seventh month, risks pushing oil prices even higher, according to experts.
Daan Struyven, co-head of global commodities research at Goldman Sachs, told CNBC it’s “definitely plausible” for oil prices to surge above $120 a barrel, if active hostilities continue.
Iran-backed Houthis escalate regional instability
Meanwhile, the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen contributed to the regional instability by launching attacks on four cities in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, targeting oil infrastructure.
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said 73 people had been injured in the strikes.
The attacks came after weeks of escalation between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government of Yemen, shattering a four-year informal cease-fire in the country's civil war.
“The U.S. has a very strong defensive military relationship with Saudi Arabia, and we’re watching those events very closely. It’s been going on for some time,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday.
The renewed fighting threatens to further disrupt shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical trade route off the Arabian Peninsula for oil and global commerce.
U.S.-Iran negotiations at a standstill, with no timeline to end war
Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, an Iranian negotiator and Parliament Speaker, told lawmakers on Sunday that the era of “proportionate responses” to American attacks had come to an end, according to state media.
Trump has said he's "not trying to force Iran to the bargaining table" and "couldn’t care less if they sign a worthless, to them, agreement." In a Sept. 1 message shared via Truth Social, he claimed the U.S. has "almost total control" of the Strait and pointed to Iran's suffering economy as evidence his approach was working.
Rosemary Kelanic, director of the Middle East program at Defense Priorities, tells TIME the current stalemate is a way for both countries to demonstrate their power and test each other’s limits.
“One way to think about war is that it's a disagreement over the balance of power and who would win a conflict,” she says. “The United States and Iran haven't figured out yet where each other's limits are, and they both think that they have to convince the other side that their position is stronger than the other.”
The two countries signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on June 17, but the pact fell apart, with Washington and Tehran seemingly adopting different interpretations of the language used in the interim agreement.
Kelanic says that, as the conflict currently stands, each exchange of tit-for-tat strikes is “disproportionately bad for the U.S. because Iran can show us that they can continue to strike ships" in and around the Persian Gulf.
“They can continue to strike U.S. bases in Jordan and elsewhere. The U.S. can continue to defend, but the cost of defending is much higher because we're using these interceptors,” she tells TIME.
The Iran war has cost the U.S. at least $37.5 billion, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in July, prompting criticism from Democratic lawmakers who have pointed to the rising costs of gas, groceries, and more for American consumers.

sources.news_title: US Military Says It Destroyed 5 More Iranian Oil Tankers After Missile Attacks on Navy Warship
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. military said it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday in response to the latest attacks on its warships and Tehran hit back at American targets in Jordan, the latest burst of back-and-forth strikes that have lurched the sides back toward open hostilities in a more than 6-month-old war.
Following the American strikes, Iran launched missiles toward U.S. targets in Jordan, Iranian state-run media said. Jordan’s military said its air defense systems intercepted 18 ballistic missiles launched toward its territory and two others fell in places where no one lives. It said it has no reports of casualties. Jordan is a staunch U.S. ally that hosts American forces, making the kingdom’s military bases a target of repeat Iranian strikes. U.S. Central Command said it had no information to offer.
The latest strikes are part of a dual economic and military approach by President Donald Trump as he struggles to bring an end to the war. The Trump administration on Tuesday also imposed sanctions on additional elements of Iran’s aviation industry, targeting more than two dozen commercial and private airlines as well as foreign cargo service providers, in its new push to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.
Both the U.S. and Iran are seeking to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz, where about one-fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war began. Rising energy prices are posing political problems for Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the November midterm elections. A barrel of international standard Brent crude briefly climbed as high as $99.46 on Tuesday.
The U.S. forces also destroyed three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday after Iran’s Revolutionary Guards tried to attack a U.S. aircraft carrier and destroyer with ballistic missiles, warning that it would, “if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.” Iran later said it planned to announce a new “exclusion zone” near the Strait of Hormuz aimed at vessels intending to transit.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. will not allow Iran’s attacks to go unanswered.
“Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships. And for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers. And I think you’ll see that again today,” Rubio told reporters Tuesday when asked about the latest attacks in Iran while on a trip to Colombia.
Danny Citrinowicz, an Iran expert at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies, warned that such back-and-forth strikes can only risk more retaliation and further impact to the global economy.
“There is no kinetic solution to the Strait of Hormuz problem,” he said on social media. “Every attempt to impose one only brings Washington and Tehran closer to an escalation that may become increasingly difficult to control.”
U.S. Central Command said the military struck the tankers on Tuesday after the Revolutionary Guards targeted a Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days. “The U.S. warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed,” it said in a statement.
It said the Iranian tankers destroyed on Tuesday were the Kivik, Charminar, Horizon 1 and the Riesco in the Gulf of Oman. The U.S. military also destroyed the vessel Derya, which was located near Kharg Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The statement said the crews of the five vessels were told to abandoned ship before the attacks.
Iranian state television also reported the U.S. strikes, saying U.S. forces attacked Iranian oil tankers near the southern port of Jask and near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf. It said the crews were evacuated.
An Iranian state TV reporter in Jask said an Iranian tanker was struck near the coast of Yekbeni. State TV later reported that the U.S. military attacked a second tanker near waters off Jask. Separately, state television reported that another Iranian tanker was attacked in the Kharg Island anchorage area.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy on Tuesday had warned crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels, saying the ships could be targeted in retaliation for U.S. attacks on Iranian tankers. It accused Kuwait and Bahrain of hosting U.S. forces and assisting in the attacks.
A U.S. blockade of Iranian ports has squeezed the country’s economy by limiting its oil exports, while the American military has been helping a limited number of ships transit on a route through the Strait of Hormuz off Oman. Tehran wants ships to follow a route that it chooses through the strait, which was considered an international waterway before the war.

CENTCOM Destroys Five IRGC-Linked Oil Tankers In Largest Single Naval Strike Of The Hormuz Conflict - Armed Forces Press
sources.text:
U.S. Central Command confirmed Tuesday that American forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers in the latest round of retaliatory strikes in the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman – the most significant single naval engagement of the ongoing conflict with Tehran.
CENTCOM confirmed the four tankers destroyed in the Gulf of Oman were M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1, and M/T Riesco. A fifth tanker, M/T Derya, was destroyed in the Persian Gulf near Kharg Island — Iran’s main oil export terminal, operated by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
The strikes were launched in retaliation for a series of failed Iranian missile attacks against U.S. guided-missile destroyers DDG-119 and DDG-53 over the preceding 48 hours. U.S. Navy air defense systems intercepted all incoming missiles. Iran’s state-run media claimed IRGC forces also struck eight oil tankers in the strait, though those reports were not independently confirmed.
A separate Iranian missile salvo targeting U.S. military positions in Jordan was also repelled Tuesday. U.S. officials described the attack as “ineffective,” with no missiles reaching their targets.
Brent crude continued rising on news of the strike, as tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — the world’s most critical energy chokepoint — remained severely disrupted. The five tankers destroyed represent the single largest loss of Iranian commercial shipping assets since the conflict began in 2026. CENTCOM said the strikes were “designed to impose costs on Iran for continued attacks on international shipping and U.S. forces.”
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi condemned the strikes as “aggression on Iranian sovereign assets” and vowed a “proportionate and decisive” response.
The Pentagon has not altered rules of engagement, with officials maintaining that the current posture is calibrated to impose costs on IRGC assets without expanding the conflict beyond maritime and energy-related targets.

sources.news_title: UCENTCOM says US forces destroyed 5 Iranian tankers after attacks on American warship
sources.text:
UCENTCOM says US forces destroyed 5 Iranian tankers after attacks on American warship
WASHINGTON — US forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and near Kharg Island after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days, the US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on Tuesday.
"The US warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed," it said in a statement.
Iran responded to attacks on its tankers by firing missiles at US forces stationed at the Al Azraq base in Jordan. It also claimed additional strikes on at least two US vessels and eight tankers in the region, saying the assaults caused “great damage”.
In a separate post on the US social media platform X, CENTCOM said the Iranian tanker M/T Riesco sank in the Gulf of Oman after being destroyed by US forces in response to the attempted IRGC attacks.
CENTCOM released footage showing the vessel sinking, saying it was destroyed on Sept. 8.
The exchange of fire comes amid escalating tensions in the Gulf six months into the US and Israel’s war on Iran, with Tehran closing the Strait of Hormuz and Washington enforcing a naval blockade on Iranian ports.
The hostilities drove oil prices to $99.49 a barrel in early trading on Wednesday.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said earlier Tuesday that Iran would continue to lose tankers for every attempt it makes to strike US naval vessels.
"Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers. And I think you'll see that again today," Rubio told reporters during his visit to Colombia.
Iran's Tasnim news agency reported that a tanker was struck near Kharg Island's anchorage area, with no casualties reported and the crew evacuated.
The state broadcaster IRIB separately reported that two oil tankers were attacked near the port of Jask, with their crews evacuated to shore by lifeboat.
The developments came amid heightened tensions between Iran and the US over the Strait of Hormuz, despite the signing of a memorandum in June that envisioned a deal to reopen the strategic waterway as a prelude to a wider peace deal.

sources.news_title: U.S. Destroys 5 Iranian Oil Tankers After IRGC Targets American Warship With Ballistic Missiles
sources.text:
U.S. Destroys 5 Iranian Oil Tankers After IRGC Targets American Warship With Ballistic Missiles
The US Central Command forces have destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday (Sept 8, 2026).
The attack comes after Iran targeted a US Navy warship in two separate attacks over two days.
The American warship avoided both missile attacks and remained on patrol in regional waters. CENTCOM said no U.S. personnel were injured.
The four targeted vessels were M/T Charminar, M/T Kaviz, M/T Horizon 1, and M/T Riesco.
Before the strikes, U.S. forces instructed the crews to leave the tankers, CENTCOM said. The vessels were left inoperable after being struck.
The operation followed similar U.S. action on Sept. 5, when CENTCOM forces destroyed three Iranian oil tankers after the IRGC attempted to attack a U.S. aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer.
CENTCOM said none of the IRGC’s attempts to strike U.S. Navy warships had succeeded.
According to the U.S. military, the five tankers were linked to a multibillion-dollar network that provides funding for the IRGC and its regional proxies. CENTCOM also said Iran was unable to defend the vessels.
CENTCOM forces destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers, Sept. 8, after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days. The U.S. warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and… pic.twitter.com/Gi8a2tloN1
— U.S. Central Command (@CENTCOM) September 8, 2026
After the tanker strikes, Iran fired ballistic missiles at Jordan and told tanker crews near ports and piers in Kuwait and Bahrain to leave their ships, Iranian state television reported.
The Armed Forces of Jordan said air defences shot down 18 of the 20 missiles fired towards the country. Two others landed in areas with no population.
No casualties were reported. Jordanian authorities said specialist teams were working at the sites where the missiles landed to secure missile fragments and other debris.
Ali Abdollahi, the chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces had previously said Tehran would target U.S. military facilities across the region if Iranian tankers came under attack.
Oil prices rose following the strikes near Kharg Island, an important Iranian crude-export hub. Brent crude moved close to $100 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate traded near $95.
