sources.news_title: Iran warns people to 'evacuate' in Middle East as massive military strikes coming
sources.text:
Iran has issued an urgent warning for ships to leave waters near Kuwait and Bahrain as Tehran vows retaliation against American military sites across the region.
According to a report from Express.co.uk, Iran’s Navy broadcast a stark alert through state television, telling crews of oil tankers in the area to abandon their vessels immediately.
The message accused the United States of attacking several Iranian oil tankers and declared that ports in Kuwait and Bahrain, which it said host “these terrorists,” would themselves become targets.
“All oil tankers in the Kuwait and Bahrain area must be evacuated immediately,” the Iranian broadcast stated. “Given the atrocities of the US terrorist army in targeting several Iranian oil tankers, we warn all oil tanker crews in the vicinity of the Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports—which host these terrorists and are complicit in their crimes—to immediately abandon their vessels, whether at anchor or alongside the docks, as they will be targeted.”
The warning landed only days after Kuwait reported that its air defenses were engaging incoming missiles and drones. Kuwaiti authorities described the assaults as “hostile missile and drone attacks, following the sinful Iranian aggression.” Officials there also cautioned residents that any explosions they heard were likely the sound of intercepts, urging the public to follow official safety instructions.
The latest Iranian threat followed U.S. strikes on Tuesday against targets near Kharg Island and Jask. Iran’s Tasnim news agency, linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, confirmed that a tanker was struck by a missile roughly four miles from Kharg Island and reported no casualties.
Those operations came after the United States said it had hit three Iranian oil tankers over the weekend, destroying one, in response to earlier attacks on American Navy ships.
The IRGC has already claimed it seized one of the U.S. military’s most advanced unmanned submarines in the Strait of Hormuz, describing the capture as the result of a “complex intelligence and operational action” at the entrance to the vital shipping lane. Iran’s top security official has also announced that a new restricted zone outside the Strait of Hormuz will be declared in the coming days.
With oil routes, U.S. bases, and regional ports now openly threatened, the confrontation that began with weekend tanker strikes has rapidly expanded into a broader contest over control of the Gulf.

sources.news_title: U.S. Strikes Iranian Oil Tankers Near Kharg Island and Jask as Tehran Threatens Wider Retaliation
sources.text:
U.S. forces targeted multiple Iranian oil tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps on Tuesday after an attempted missile attack on an American warship, escalating Washington’s campaign to pressure Tehran as Iran threatened retaliation against U.S. bases and regional shipping.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom.
U.S. forces launched a new round of strikes against multiple Iranian oil tankers Tuesday, including targets near the critical oil-export hub of Kharg Island and the port of Jask, as Washington intensified military and economic pressure on Tehran and Iranian officials threatened a broader retaliation against American forces and interests across the Middle East.
A U.S. official said the targeted tankers were connected to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and that the strikes followed an attempted Iranian ballistic missile attack on a U.S. Navy warship Monday. The missile did not hit the American vessel, and U.S. forces subsequently moved against the tankers to demonstrate that attacks on American military assets would carry additional costs.
The U.S. military operation remained underway Tuesday, according to the official. The Associated Press separately reported that American forces had struck multiple Iranian oil tankers following renewed Iranian missile attacks against a U.S. warship.
The latest strikes represent another escalation in a confrontation that has increasingly focused on Iran’s ability to export oil and finance the IRGC. U.S. officials said the tanker attacks are part of a broader effort to squeeze Tehran economically while the Trump administration increases pressure on Iran over its nuclear program.
U.S. Central Command carried out strikes near Kharg Island and Jask, with an American official saying Iranian crude carriers were among the targets and that U.S. forces sought to sink or disable them.
Kharg Island is a central hub for Iranian crude exports, making vessels operating around the island particularly significant to Tehran’s energy economy. More than 20 Iranian tankers were in the area earlier Tuesday, TankerTrackers co-founder Sam Madani told Fox News.
Explosions were reported near both Kharg Island and Jask. Iranian state media initially said the origin of the blasts and the extent of any damage were unclear. Reuters also reported explosions in the two areas, citing the Mehr and Fars news agencies. A ballistic missile was separately reported to have been launched from Jask.
The strikes came only days after CENTCOM announced that U.S. forces had destroyed or disabled three IRGC-linked crude oil tankers following Iranian ballistic missile attacks directed toward two U.S. Navy warships. CENTCOM said Saturday that no American personnel were injured in those attacks.
Iran signaled before Tuesday’s latest operation that it was preparing to respond.
Iranian military spokesman Ebrahim Zolfaghari said earlier Tuesday that three Iranian tankers had received warnings that U.S. attacks were imminent. He said any strikes against the vessels would trigger Iranian attacks against American military bases and other U.S. interests throughout the region.
The IRGC subsequently warned that ships located in Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports hosting American forces could become targets in retaliation for U.S. attacks on Iranian oil tankers. The IRGC Navy urged crews aboard potentially affected vessels to evacuate, according to Iranian state media and Reuters.
Iranian armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi issued a broader warning, saying attacks against Iranian ships could prompt strikes against U.S. military installations throughout the region, according to a statement distributed by Iran’s state news agency.
The threats come as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has fallen to its lowest level since May amid the widening confrontation. Traffic through the strategic waterway slowed further this week after Tehran warned that renewed U.S. attacks would provoke retaliation against regional energy infrastructure and American interests.
The Trump administration has been simultaneously expanding economic measures intended to isolate Iran. U.S. officials have said the objective is to increase pressure on Tehran to meet American demands concerning its nuclear program while limiting the government’s ability to generate revenue through oil and other sectors.
Tuesday’s tanker strikes fit directly into that effort. A U.S. official described the operations against Iranian crude carriers as “part of that pressure campaign,” noting that oil exports remain a crucial source of income for Tehran.
The military pressure has been accompanied by additional sanctions. The Treasury Department on Tuesday announced a sweeping new package targeting Iran’s aviation sector and companies accused of supporting its procurement networks, another step in Washington’s effort to restrict Tehran’s access to international commerce.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi responded by arguing that Washington’s longstanding strategy of economic and military pressure had failed.
“After 47 years of sanctions, the U.S. went to war with Iran on behalf of Israel,” Araghchi said in a post on X.
“The fallout has been disastrous for America, including its standing worldwide,” he added.
“After failing to achieve its aims through sanctions or war, Washington’s ‘novel’ solution is…more sanctions. Seriously?” Araghchi said.
Iran’s warnings have heightened concern that the latest tanker strikes could expand beyond direct exchanges between American and Iranian forces. The IRGC’s references to vessels in Bahrain and Kuwait are particularly significant because both Gulf states host U.S. military personnel and facilities.
The continuing hostilities are also placing greater strain on global energy markets. Crude prices rose to six-week highs Tuesday as fighting expanded across the region, including attacks by Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi energy facilities. Brent crude approached $100 per barrel as traders assessed the possibility of prolonged disruptions to oil production and shipping routes.
Washington’s campaign against Iranian tankers has increasingly targeted what U.S. officials describe as a shadow shipping network that generates revenue for the IRGC and its regional partners.
Tuesday’s strikes appear to extend that strategy from economic sanctions and maritime restrictions toward repeated direct military attacks against vessels associated with Iran’s oil trade.
The development came amid other diplomatic disputes surrounding the broader Middle East conflict. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar separately announced countermeasures Tuesday in response to new sanctions imposed by British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, describing Britain’s action as part of two years of unilateral moves against Israel.
For the immediate U.S.-Iran confrontation, however, the focus has shifted increasingly to the Gulf and Iran’s oil infrastructure.
American officials say the latest strikes were retaliation for Iran’s attempted attack on a U.S. warship and part of an economic campaign intended to weaken Tehran’s access to oil revenue. Iran, meanwhile, has warned that further attacks on its tankers could bring strikes against American military bases and ships using ports across the Gulf, raising the prospect that the confrontation could widen further beyond Iranian waters.

sources.news_title: US strikes Iranian tankers plus other key Mideast news
sources.text:
The U.S. on Tuesday destroyed five Iranian tankers in response to attempted missile attacks on a Navy warship, marking the latest tit-for-tat strikes between the two countries. Earlier, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia ignited fires at several oil facilities and wounded dozens of people. That raised the stakes in renewed fighting between a U.S. ally and an Iranian proxy just days after deadly clashes in Iran, Lebanon and Gaza.
Meanwhile, Britain's government said it is banning goods from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Israel responded by saying it will close the British consulate in Jerusalem.
Here’s a look at the latest news in the Middle East. Full coverage can be found here.
US destroys 5 Iranian tankers after attempted attacks on Navy warship
U.S. Central Command said in a social media post that it destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers after Tehran fired missiles at a U.S. warship twice over two days.
It marked the latest tit-for-tat strikes as Washington and Tehran lurch back toward fighting during more than six months of war.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy has warned crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels, saying the ships could be targeted in retaliation for U.S. attacks on Iranian tankers.
The warning, carried by Iranian state television, said the U.S. military had targeted several Iranian oil tankers. It accused Kuwait and Bahrain of hosting U.S. forces and assisting in the attacks.
Iran strikes US targets in Jordan in tit-for-tat retaliation
Iran has launched missiles toward U.S. targets in Jordan, Iranian state-run media said, following the latest American strikes.
It’s the latest tit-for-tat retaliation after the U.S. military said it destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers following two attacks on a U.S. warship by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard over the past two days.
U.S. Central Command, when asked about the strikes on the Jordanian air base, said it had no information to offer.
Jordan’s military said its air defense systems intercepted 18 ballistic missiles launched toward its territory and two others fell in places where people do not live. It says it has no reports of casualties. Jordan is a staunch U.S. ally that hosts American forces, making the kingdom’s military bases a target of repeat Iranian strikes.
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia injure at least 73
A wave of Houthi attacks ignited fires at several oil facilities and utilities in Saudi Arabia’s southern region, injuring at least 73 people, officials said.
The attacks early Tuesday marked a major escalation in the renewed conflict between an important U.S. ally and the Iranian-backed rebels in Yemen. They follow weeks of intensifying clashes between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen, which shattered a four-year truce in the country’s civil war.
The flare-up brings further instability to a region scarred by nearly three years of wars and threatens to squeeze shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical trade route that has helped cushion the blow from Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz.
The attacks hit “civilian and economic facilities” in the Saudi cities of Abha, Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait, said Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen.
UK announces Israeli settlement sanctions
The U.K. announced it is banning trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, saying an expansion program there is endangering efforts to establish a Palestinian state.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said that “settler terrorists” are carrying out “ethnic cleansing” of Palestinians. He said the U.K. will ban imports of all goods from the settlements as well as some services.
Israel will close the British consulate in Jerusalem, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said on Tuesday. He said Israel will also expel U.K. representatives from a joint military center monitoring the Gaza ceasefire and end U.K. training of the Palestinian Authority’s security forces in the West Bank.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu 's government has presided over a surge of settlement construction in the West Bank, which Israel seized in the 1967 Mideast war and which would make up the main part of a future Palestinian state.
The international community considers the settlements illegal or illegitimate, and the Palestinians say they are the main barrier to lasting peace. Netanyahu’s government views the West Bank as the biblical and historical homeland of the Jewish people and opposes the creation of a Palestinian state.
Iran says it seized a US underwater drone
Iran’s navy captured one of the U.S. military’s underwater drones at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, Iranian state television reported, saying the unmanned vessel had been “seized as a prize.”
Asked about the report, U.S. Central Command spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins said that an Anduril Dive-LD drone malfunctioned “more than a day ago” while surveying waters in the region and that the U.S. military no longer had possession of it.
Hawkins said the drone was a defective, older model that “neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment.”
“It was in a commercially available configuration so we aren’t concerned,” Hawkins said.
A child is among 2 people killed by gunfire in Gaza
A child was among at least two people killed on Tuesday by Israeli troops in Gaza, according to hospital officials.
A 10-year-old boy died after forces opened fire near tents sheltering displaced Palestinians east of Khan Younis, according to Nasser Hospital. It said Israeli fire also killed a 69-year-old man south of Khan Younis.
Hospital officials said both victims died on the Palestinian side of the “yellow line” that separates areas of Gaza occupied by the Israeli military. Palestinians near the dividing line have faced heightened danger from Israeli fire.
Separately, an Israeli strike in Nuseirat refugee camp wounded 10 people, Al-Awda Hospital said.
Residents in several areas said they received evacuation warnings, followed by strikes in Khan Younis, Bureij refugee camp and Gaza City.
The Israeli military did not immediately comment on the attacks.
___
This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.
The Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. military said it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday in response to the latest attacks on its warships and Tehran hit back at American targets in Jordan, the latest burst of back-and-forth strikes that have lurched the sides back toward open hostilities in a more than 6-month-old war.
Following the American strikes, Iran launched missiles toward U.S. targets in Jordan, Iranian state-run media said. Jordan’s military said its air defense systems intercepted 18 ballistic missiles launched toward its territory and two others fell in places where no one lives. It said it has no reports of casualties. Jordan is a staunch U.S. ally that hosts American forces, making the kingdom’s military bases a target of repeat Iranian strikes. U.S. Central Command said it had no information to offer.
The latest strikes are part of a dual economic and military approach by President Donald Trump as he struggles to bring an end to the war. The Trump administration on Tuesday also imposed sanctions on additional elements of Iran’s aviation industry, targeting more than two dozen commercial and private airlines as well as foreign cargo service providers, in its new push to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.
Both the U.S. and Iran are seeking to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz, where about one-fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war began. Rising energy prices are posing political problems for Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the November midterm elections. A barrel of international standard Brent crude briefly climbed as high as $99.46 on Tuesday.
The U.S. forces also destroyed three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday after Iran’s Revolutionary Guards tried to attack a U.S. aircraft carrier and destroyer with ballistic missiles, warning that it would, “if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.” Iran later said it planned to announce a new “exclusion zone” near the Strait of Hormuz aimed at vessels intending to transit.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. will not allow Iran’s attacks to go unanswered.
“Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships. And for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers. And I think you’ll see that again today,” Rubio told reporters Tuesday when asked about the latest attacks in Iran while on a trip to Colombia.
Danny Citrinowicz, an Iran expert at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies, warned that such back-and-forth strikes can only risk more retaliation and further impact to the global economy.
“There is no kinetic solution to the Strait of Hormuz problem,” he said on social media. “Every attempt to impose one only brings Washington and Tehran closer to an escalation that may become increasingly difficult to control.”
U.S. Central Command said the military struck the tankers on Tuesday after the Revolutionary Guards targeted a Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days. “The U.S. warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed,” it said in a statement.
It said the Iranian tankers destroyed on Tuesday were the Kivik, Charminar, Horizon 1 and the Riesco in the Gulf of Oman. The U.S. military also destroyed the vessel Derya, which was located near Kharg Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The statement said the crews of the five vessels were told to abandoned ship before the attacks.
Iranian state television also reported the U.S. strikes, saying U.S. forces attacked Iranian oil tankers near the southern port of Jask and near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf. It said the crews were evacuated.
An Iranian state TV reporter in Jask said an Iranian tanker was struck near the coast of Yekbeni. State TV later reported that the U.S. military attacked a second tanker near waters off Jask. Separately, state television reported that another Iranian tanker was attacked in the Kharg Island anchorage area.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy on Tuesday had warned crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels, saying the ships could be targeted in retaliation for U.S. attacks on Iranian tankers. It accused Kuwait and Bahrain of hosting U.S. forces and assisting in the attacks.
A U.S. blockade of Iranian ports has squeezed the country’s economy by limiting its oil exports, while the American military has been helping a limited number of ships transit on a route through the Strait of Hormuz off Oman. sources.news_title: US-Iran tanker attacks signal a dangerous new phase in war
sources.text:
At least seven oil tankers have been struck in and beyond the Persian Gulf since Tuesday evening local time, as the United States and Iran step up tanker attacks in what could mark a dangerous new phase in the war.
The escalation led global oil prices to rise briefly above $100 per barrel for the first time since July. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, rose 2.3% before falling back slightly.
Late Tuesday, the US military struck five Iranian tankers, sinking one, after Iran fired ballistic missiles at a US Navy warship.
Four crude oil carriers in the Gulf of Oman and one near Kharg Island – a hub for Iranian oil exports in the Persian Gulf – were struck, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said.
One of the ships, identified as the M/T Riesco, is seen on fire and sinking in the Gulf of Oman in a video posted to X by the military. US forces instructed the crews of the vessels they targeted to abandon ship prior to striking, CENTCOM said.
Iran retaliated by firing a barrage of missiles toward regional US ally Jordan, saying it was targeting Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, a key facility used by US forces.
The barrage was ineffective in face of integrated air and missile defenses, a US official told CNN.
The Jordanian army said its air defenses dealt with 20 ballistic missiles, 18 of them successfully destroyed, with two falling in unpopulated areas.
On Wednesday, two tankers in the Gulf were struck by drones. One was off Dubai’s coast, the other in Iraqi waters.
A seafarer was killed in an incident involving the Gibraltar-flagged oil products tanker Hercules Star while at anchorage off Dubai, the vessel’s charterer, Peninsula, said on Wednesday. It gave no cause of death.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) center said earlier that a vessel in the same area was seen listing, indicating that it could be taking on water after an attack from an “unknown projectile.
Further north, a Panama-flagged tanker was struck by an unknown source in Iraqi waters, causing damage to the vessel’s hull, according to the Iraqi Ministry of Transport.
The incident caused no casualties or injuries among the crew, the ministry said.
There’s been no claim of responsibility for the attacks on the two tankers.
But Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had warned “all crews aboard oil tankers in the vicinity of ports in Kuwait and Bahrain – which host these (US) terrorists and are partners in their hostile actions – to immediately leave their vessels, whether they are at anchor or docked at the ports, as the vessels will be targeted.”
The US strikes were in response to Iranian attempts to attack a US Navy ship over the past two days. The US ship evaded the missiles and was continuing to patrol regional waters, CENTCOM said, adding that “no American personnel were harmed.”
The exchange of strikes comes as the US has focused its strategy on ramping up economic pressure on the Tehran regime, while conducting escort operations for commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz and maintaining its naval blockade on Iranian ports.
Over the weekend US forces hit three Iranian crude oil carriers in response to an Iranian attempt to attack a US aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer.
‘Pattern of gradual escalation’
Iran’s repeated attempts to attack US warships and the increased “quality and quantity” of the missiles it fired at US targets in the region showed “a pattern of gradual escalation,” said Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, on X.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, during his trip to Colombia, warned Tehran that the US would respond every time Iran targeted its naval ships.
“Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships and for every time they do that, or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” he told reporters in the city of Barranquilla.
Iran has also announced that it will expand its maritime restriction zone in the Persian Gulf region.
A spokesman for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), General Hossein Mohebbi, said the expanded zone would start “approximately from the direction of Chabahar,” an Iranian port city on the Gulf of Oman, and would include “another part of the Arabian Sea along the route leading to the Strait of Hormuz.”
Exact coordinates would be announced later, he said.
Tehran has sought to maintain leverage over transits through the strait as a way to keep oil prices high and put pressure on the Trump administration.
Gasoline prices in the US climbed to a fresh three-month high above $4.15 a gallon on Tuesday.
On Wednesday Trump said he expects Iran will abandon its war effort after the US midterm elections — and that American gas prices are unlikely to come down before then.
This story has been updated with additional information.
CNN’s Eleni Giokos, Eyad Kourdi, Thomas Bordeaux and Yasha Saebi contributed reporting.

sources.news_title: US strikes Iranian tankers, IRGC vows to target oil vessels in Kuwait and Bahrain
sources.text:
US strikes Iranian tankers, IRGC vows to target oil vessels in Kuwait and Bahrain
US military attacked have struck Iranian oil tankers following further attempted missile attacks on a US Navy warship. In response, Revolutionary Guards said that oil vessels in Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports hosting American forces will be targeted in retaliation.
US forces have struck multiple Iranian oil tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) following further attempted missile attacks on a US Navy warship, news agency Reuters reported, citing a US official. Iranian media reported multiple strikes, with Tasnim news agency saying a US missile hit an Iranian tanker about 4 miles (6 km) from the oil hub of Kharg Island, while state broadcaster reported that a second tanker was attacked near Jask in the Gulf of Oman.
The latest escalation follows a second wave of Iranian ballistic missile attacks against US Navy ships on Monday, US officials told The Wall Street Journal. The American military has not publicly acknowledged the attack. No US vessels were hit in either the Monday strikes or the earlier weekend attack, which targeted a US aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer. US officials said the repeated attacks have raised concerns over Iran's increasingly sophisticated missile capabilities and possible technical assistance from China or Russia.
IRAN WARNS OIL VESSELS IN KUWAIT, BAHRAIN
In response, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said early Wednesday that oil vessels in Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports hosting American forces will be targeted in retaliation. The Guards Navy warned crews aboard the vessels to evacuate, according to a statement carried by Iranian state media, sharply raising the stakes around key Gulf shipping routes.
The US has also imposed sanctions on 36 Iranian entities, including 27 airlines, in an effort to further isolate Iran's aviation sector.
This follows a sharp exchange of retaliatory strikes on Saturday. The US military said it "permanently disabled" two Iran-linked oil tankers—one near Kharg Island, Iran's main oil export terminal and "completely destroyed" a third in the Gulf of Oman. US Central Command (Centcom) said the tankers belonged to a multi-billion-dollar shadow network that funds Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and its proxies.
Centcom reported that the action came after Iranian forces launched multiple unprovoked ballistic-missile attacks on a US aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer earlier that day; both warships successfully evaded the strikes and no American personnel were harmed.
Iranian state media confirmed the US tanker strikes and claimed the IRGC had retaliated by attacking three US-affiliated vessels as well as three oil tankers traveling an "unauthorised" route through the Strait of Hormuz.
The latest round of exchanges is the most intense since fighting resumed a week earlier, ending roughly a month of relative calm. A 60-day ceasefire formally expired last month with no broader diplomatic settlement in sight. The conflict, which began with wide-ranging US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, has seen the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed to regular traffic, driving up global energy prices.
US President Donald Trump has described the ongoing fighting as "small potatoes" and "intermittent," insisting it is a "military conflict" rather than a full-scale war. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wrote on social media Saturday: "It's simple: if Iran shoots at US ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers." Trump has not yet commented on the weekend tanker strikes or the subsequent Monday attacks.
WAR EXPANDS IN THE MIDDLE EAST
The conflict in the Middle East is spreading further into the Gulf, with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis launching attacks on four cities in southern Saudi Arabia on Tuesday. The strikes wounded more than 70 people and sparked fires at oil-related facilities, marking a significant escalation in attacks on the US ally.
The Houthis, who control much of Yemen's populated territory, including the capital Sanaa, said they carried out a large-scale operation inside Saudi Arabia. Their forces used drones and missiles to target a Saudi airbase in Khamis Mushait and facilities linked to state oil giant Saudi Aramco in Abha, Najran and Jazan.
Satellite imagery from NASA showed heavy black smoke above the Jazan refinery, while another plume was seen rising from an oil distribution facility in Abha.
Saudi authorities confirmed fires at the targeted locations and said 73 people were injured, including women and children. The scale of the casualties suggested the strikes were among the most serious attacks on Saudi Arabia since the wider US-Israeli war against Iran began in February.
The escalation happened after fighting resumed in the Gulf following a month-long lull in August. Iran and the US have exchanged fire, pushing global oil prices back towards the $100-a-barrel mark reached at the height of the conflict.

U.S. Hits Iranian Tankers Following Missile Fire At Navy Warship - Tampa Free Press
sources.text:
The United States struck multiple Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday following attempted missile attacks on an American Navy warship, a U.S. official told The Associated Press, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations. The AP was first to report the strikes.
The action follows strikes on Saturday, when the U.S. military hit three Iranian tankers after Navy ships were targeted with ballistic missiles. At the time, Washington issued a warning that it would, “if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.”
In response to Tuesday’s strikes, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy warned commercial tanker crews near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to abandon their ships immediately, stating that the vessels “will be targeted” whether anchored or docked.
Iranian state television reported that the Revolutionary Guard accused both Kuwait and Bahrain of assisting the U.S. operations by hosting American military forces. Iran also stated plans to establish an “exclusion zone” near the Strait of Hormuz to regulate transiting vessels.
Alongside the maritime operations, the Trump administration on Tuesday introduced new sanctions aimed at isolating Tehran from remaining trading partners. The measures target over two dozen commercial and private airlines, along with foreign cargo service providers.
Control over the Strait of Hormuz remains a primary focus for both nations, as the waterway carried roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil supply prior to the outbreak of the six-month conflict. A U.S. naval blockade continues to limit Iranian exports from its domestic ports while escorting select commercial ships along a designated transit route off the coast of Oman. Tehran has contested this arrangement, demanding that vessels utilize an alternate route under its direction.
The escalating maritime dispute coincided with a rise in global energy markets on Tuesday, with Brent crude briefly climbing to $99.46 per barrel ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections.

sources.news_title: US strikes more Iranian tankers after missile attacks on Navy warship
sources.text:
US military says it destroyed 5 Iranian tankers over past 2 days
WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. military said it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday in response to the latest attacks on its warships and Tehran hit back at American targets in Jordan, the latest burst of back-and-forth strikes that have lurched the sides back toward open hostilities in a more than 6-month-old war.
Following the American strikes, Iran launched missiles toward U.S. targets in Jordan, Iranian state-run media said. Jordan’s military said its air defense systems intercepted 18 ballistic missiles launched toward its territory and two others fell in places where no one lives. It said it has no reports of casualties. Jordan is a staunch U.S. ally that hosts American forces, making the kingdom’s military bases a target of repeat Iranian strikes. U.S. Central Command said it had no information to offer.
The latest strikes are part of a dual economic and military approach by President Donald Trump as he struggles to bring an end to the war. The Trump administration on Tuesday also imposed sanctions on additional elements of Iran’s aviation industry, targeting more than two dozen commercial and private airlines as well as foreign cargo service providers, in its new push to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.
Both the U.S. and Iran are seeking to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz, where about one-fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war began. Rising energy prices are posing political problems for Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the November midterm elections. A barrel of international standard Brent crude briefly climbed as high as $99.46 on Tuesday.
The U.S. forces also destroyed three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday after Iran’s Revolutionary Guards tried to attack a U.S. aircraft carrier and destroyer with ballistic missiles, warning that it would, “if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.” Iran later said it planned to announce a new “exclusion zone” near the Strait of Hormuz aimed at vessels intending to transit.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. will not allow Iran’s attacks to go unanswered.
“Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships. And for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers. And I think you’ll see that again today,” Rubio told reporters Tuesday when asked about the latest attacks in Iran while on a trip to Colombia.
Danny Citrinowicz, an Iran expert at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies, warned that such back-and-forth strikes can only risk more retaliation and further impact to the global economy.
“There is no kinetic solution to the Strait of Hormuz problem,” he said on social media. “Every attempt to impose one only brings Washington and Tehran closer to an escalation that may become increasingly difficult to control.”
U.S. Central Command said the military struck the tankers on Tuesday after the Revolutionary Guards targeted a Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days. “The U.S. warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed,” it said in a statement.
It said the Iranian tankers destroyed on Tuesday were the Kivik, Charminar, Horizon 1 and the Riesco in the Gulf of Oman. The U.S. military also destroyed the vessel Derya, which was located near Kharg Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The statement said the crews of the five vessels were told to abandoned ship before the attacks.
Iranian state television also reported the U.S. strikes, saying U.S. forces attacked Iranian oil tankers near the southern port of Jask and near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf. It said the crews were evacuated.
An Iranian state TV reporter in Jask said an Iranian tanker was struck near the coast of Yekbeni. State TV later reported that the U.S. military attacked a second tanker near waters off Jask. Separately, state television reported that another Iranian tanker was attacked in the Kharg Island anchorage area.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy on Tuesday had warned crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels, saying the ships could be targeted in retaliation for U.S. attacks on Iranian tankers. It accused Kuwait and Bahrain of hosting U.S. forces and assisting in the attacks.
A U.S. blockade of Iranian ports has squeezed the country’s economy by limiting its oil exports, while the American military has been helping a limited number of ships transit on a route through the Strait of Hormuz off Oman. Tehran wants ships to follow a route that it chooses through the strait, which was considered an international waterway before the war.

sources.news_title: DEVELOPING: U.S. Strikes More Iranian Oil Tankers Near Kharg Island and Jask
sources.text:
U.S. forces carried out a fresh round of strikes against multiple Iranian oil tankers near Kharg Island and the southern port of Jask on Tuesday, opening another dangerous chapter in the fight over Tehran’s oil exports and the Strait of Hormuz.
The new attacks came after another attempted Iranian missile strike on a U.S. Navy warship, according to The Associated Press, which cited a U.S. official briefed on the sensitive military operation.
That makes Tuesday’s action a separate escalation from the three Iranian crude carriers hit by American forces on Saturday.
Fox News national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin reported that the latest targets included Iranian oil tankers near both Kharg Island, Iran’s main oil-export hub, and Jask, an alternative export point on the Gulf of Oman.
Senior US officials to Fox: US military has struck targets near Kharg Island and Jask.
The targets include Iranian oil tankers.
This is part of a larger effort to squeeze Iran economically. The strategy includes sinking and disabling Iranian crude oil tankers.
The precise number of vessels hit and the extent of the damage were not immediately detailed in a public statement from U.S. Central Command. Early reports circulating Tuesday said as many as three additional tankers may have been struck, but that count remained unconfirmed by the Pentagon at the time of publication.
Reports are emerging from Iranian state media that U.S. forces have struck three Iranian oil tankers, following the earlier U.S. announcement that three Iranian crude carriers were disabled or destroyed on September 5. CENTCOM said the strikes were carried out after Iran launched… pic.twitter.com/BIt5QuQlcB
— OSINTdefender (@sentdefender) September 8, 2026
Iran Threatens Retaliation Around Gulf Ports
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard responded with an unusually direct warning to crews aboard oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain. Iranian state television said the crews were told to leave their ships, whether the vessels were anchored or docked, because they could be targeted in retaliation.
That threat widens the immediate risk well beyond Iranian waters. Kuwait and Bahrain both host U.S. forces, and commercial shipping throughout the Gulf is already moving under the strain of the six-month conflict and competing American and Iranian efforts to control traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
Roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil passed through the strait before the war. The latest escalation pushed Brent crude as high as $99.46 a barrel on Tuesday, according to the AP.
A Second Round Of Tanker Strikes In Four Days
Saturday’s operation established the pattern now taking shape.
In an official release detailing the September 5 operation, CENTCOM said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched ballistic missiles toward a U.S. aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer patrolling regional waters.
The American ships successfully evaded the missiles, CENTCOM said, and no U.S. personnel were hurt in the attempted attacks.
CENTCOM then permanently disabled the M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and the M/T Stark 1 near Jask. A third unladen carrier, the M/T Kylo — also known as the Noxen — was struck in multiple critical locations and destroyed in the Gulf of Oman after its crew was directed to abandon ship.
The command described all three vessels as part of a multibillion-dollar oil network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies.
Adm. Brad Cooper warned that attacks on American ships would bring a greater economic cost against what he called Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.
The geography mattered. Kharg Island sits deep in the Persian Gulf at the center of Iran’s crude-export system, while Jask gives Tehran an outlet on the Gulf of Oman beyond the Strait of Hormuz.
By hitting carriers near both locations, U.S. forces demonstrated that the retaliation was not confined to one chokepoint or one shipping lane.
Iran is raising the stakes around the Strait of Hormuz, warning ships they could face sanctions if they enter a new restricted exclusion zone outside the critical waterway.
The announcement comes after the U.S. launched strikes on three Iranian oil tankers, which followed Iran… pic.twitter.com/27piWqDb2t
President Trump’s administration is pairing the military pressure with a broader effort to cut Tehran off from revenue. Washington imposed another round of sanctions Tuesday targeting more than two dozen Iranian commercial and private airlines, along with foreign cargo-service providers.
U.S. officials said the tanker strikes are part of the same campaign to squeeze Iran economically, not the start of a ground operation. The immediate question is how Tehran answers — and whether its threats against ships near Kuwait and Bahrain become another round of attacks.
This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

sources.news_title: US strikes Iranian tankers after attempted attack on Navy ship
sources.text:
US strikes Iranian tankers after attempted attack on Navy ship
Iran fired ballistic missiles into Jordan in response, targeting a key US air base in escalation after US aircraft destroyed five more oil tankers in Tehran’s fleet.
WASHINGTON — The US military carried out strikes on Iran’s Kharg Island in the Gulf and around the southeastern Iranian port city of Jask, east of the Strait of Hormuz, in the latest retaliatory exchange of fire between the two sides.
"American forces have struck multiple Iranian tankers tied to the IRGC in response to more attempted missile attacks on a US Navy warship," a US official told Al-Monitor.
US Central Command said following the strikes that it had destroyed five tankers: the M/Ts Derya, Horizon, Kaviz, Charminar and Riesco. The alleged Iranian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday was the second to target US Navy warships in just three days, military officials said.
The US warship that came under fire on Tuesday was not identified in a public statement by CENTCOM, which said that the ship and its crew were unharmed.
US military officials have repeatedly said they will respond if Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps continues to launch projectile attacks into the vital economic waterway.
Iran's state-aligned media reported that oil tankers were targeted by the US off Kharg Island and near Jask.
Roughly an hour prior to news of the US strikes on Monday, the spokesperson for Iran’s armed forces headquarters issued a warning that US bases in the region would again be targeted with attacks should the US military again strike Iranian oil tankers.
Iran's IRGC issued a statement early Tuesday following the US strikes, warning crews to abandon tanker vessels at ports in Kuwait and Bahrain, Iran’s Press TV reported.
The IRGC said countries hosting US forces share responsibility for the US attacks and said crews should “immediately move their vessels away from both anchorages and ports, as they will be targeted.”
The IRGC said it targeted US fighter aircraft hangars and maintenance facilities Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan with ballistic missiles in response to the US strikes. It also confirmed its forces had fired upon two US Navy guided missile destroyers, the USS Delbert D. Black and the USS John Paul Jones.
The US military began striking sanctioned Iranian oil tankers last week, expanding the scope of its typical targets following IRGC drone attacks on two Saudi tankers off the coast of Oman, and what officials said was a coordinated but thwarted Iranian missile and drone attack on a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer over the weekend.
The latest exchange of strikes over the contested waterway came hours after the Trump administration announced a sweeping tranche of economic sanctions aimed at isolating Iran's commercial airline industry.
Earlier on Monday, Iranian state media and government social media accounts claimed to have shot down a US MQ-1 Predator drone over the Strait of Hormuz after allegedly capturing an Anduril Dive-LD unmanned submarine.
A US military official speaking to Al-Monitor on condition of anonymity confirmed that an unmanned undersea drone was lost in the vicinity of Hormuz due to a malfunction “more than a day ago.”
“It was surveying regional waters in support of ongoing operations,” the official said, adding that the “defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment.”
The official did not confirm whether the US had recently lost an MQ-1 or any other model of aerial drone. The US military has reportedly lost at least three dozen MQ-series drones in the conflict, which the US and Israel initiated in February with surprise airstrikes against Iran.

U.S. Destroys Five More IRGC Tankers After Iran Targets Navy Warship
U.S. forces destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers Tuesday after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeted a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days, according to U.S. Central Command.
CENTCOM said the warship successfully evaded both attacks and continued its patrol. No American personnel were injured.
In response, U.S. forces struck the Kaviz, Charminar, Horizon 1 and Riesco in the Gulf of Oman, along with the Deryanear Iran’s Kharg Island. CENTCOM said crews were ordered to abandon the vessels before they were struck and rendered inoperable.
The strikes bring to eight the number of Iranian tankers attacked by U.S. forces since Sept. 5.
On Saturday, CENTCOM struck the Downy off Kharg Island and Stark 1 near Jask and sank the Kylo, also known as Noxen, in the Gulf of Oman. Those strikes followed Iranian ballistic missile attacks targeting a U.S. aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer.
CENTCOM says the tankers are part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network used to fund the IRGC and its regional proxies.
UK Maritime Trade Operations issued a new advisory Tuesday after receiving a report involving a merchant vessel in the strait. UKMTO said the vessel was “subject to interaction as part of ongoing military activity in the region.” Authorities are investigating the incident. The advisory did not identify the vessel or provide further details about the interaction.
The latest exchange comes as tensions around the Strait of Hormuz continue to escalate.
Earlier Tuesday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards threatened to target ships in Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports that host U.S. forces and warned crews to evacuate, according to Iranian state media.
The latest U.S. strikes suggest the tit-for-tat campaign is accelerating, with Washington increasingly targeting Iran’s oil-exporting fleet in direct response to attacks on American warships.
Iran said on Wednesday it had attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S. sank five Iranian oil tankers, in the biggest declared wave of tit-for-tat attacks on shipping by both sides since the start of the six-month-old war.
Suez Canal revenue rose 42% in July from the year earlier, as the Iran war’s effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi threats in the southern Red Sea led more ships to use the Egyptian waterway.
Iran said it will announce a new restricted zone in the Gulf in the coming days, along with maps of a new shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, as a weekend exchange of strikes on shipping sent oil prices higher on Monday.

While Operation Economic Fury and Operation Economic Outcast are hitting Iran hard in their checking accounts, the United States certainly isn't letting Iran off the military hook, either. On Tuesday, reports came out that American forces (probably) hit three Iranian oil tankers near the critical oil facilities on Kharg Island.

The post reads:
Reports are emerging from Iranian state media that U.S. forces have struck three Iranian oil tankers, following the earlier U.S. announcement that three Iranian crude carriers were disabled or destroyed on September 5. CENTCOM said the strikes were carried out after Iran launched ballistic missiles toward two U.S. Navy warships.
Just over 30 minutes ago, Iran’s Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces reportedly warned that U.S. forces had ordered crews aboard Iranian tankers to evacuate ahead of additional attacks. He also warned that any further attacks on Iranian tankers would result in Iranian attacks against U.S. bases across the region.
More to come on this situation.
Another report gives some more details:
Several explosions were reported near Iran’s Kharg Island in the Gulf, while an explosion was also heard in the southern port city of Jask, according to Iranian media.
Senior US officials told Fox that the US military had struck targets near Kharg Island and Jask, including Iranian oil tankers. The officials said the strikes were part of a broader effort to squeeze Iran economically, including plans to sink and disable Iranian crude oil tankers.
The latest strikes came after the US and Iran traded retaliatory attacks on ships on Saturday, in the latest round of strikes since fighting flared up a week ago following a month of relative calm.
Iran is said to have acknowledged the strikes.
The US military said it had “permanently disabled” two Iran-linked oil tankers, including one near Kharg Island, and “completely destroyed” a third tanker in the Gulf of Oman.
Iranian state media confirmed the strikes and said Tehran had responded by attacking three US-affiliated vessels, as well as three oil tankers traveling through the Strait of Hormuz along an “unauthorised” route.
Kharg Island is the bottleneck through which 90 percent of Iran's exported oil flows, and while it's not at all clear that's where these tankers were headed or coming from. There's no evidence that Kharg Island was engaged or hit in any way. But if the United States is serious about cutting off Iran's exports, hitting Kharg Island would be the way to go about it; but then, hitting tankers either attempting to take on oil or leaving after taking on oil would be another way of cutting that trade off without destroying the Kharg Island facilities that would be essential to rebuilding a new Iran.
There are also reports that Iran's commercial shipping ports are idle. That's another compelling argument for the certain starting down.

According to CENTCOM, the warship was targeted twice over the past two days by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The attacks caused no personnel injuries or operational damage, and the vessel remained on active patrol.
In response, US forces carried out coordinated strikes against five vessels that CENTCOM described as belonging to Iran’s state-linked maritime fleet.
“Four crude oil carriers—the M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1 and M/T Riesco—were destroyed in the Gulf of Oman, while a fifth vessel, the M/T Derya, was hit near Kharg Island,” CENTCOM said in a statement.
The US military said crews aboard the vessels had been directed to abandon ship before the strikes were carried out. The vessels were subsequently rendered inoperable.
CENTCOM identified the ships as part of a “multibillion-dollar shadow network” that it alleged helps fund the IRGC and its regional proxies.
The strikes mark the second major US operation targeting Iran’s maritime infrastructure in three days. On September 5, US forces reportedly destroyed three Iranian crude oil carriers after the IRGC attempted to attack a US aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer.
Meanwhile, Iran has launched a barrage of missiles targeting US military positions in Jordan. The IRGC has also warned tanker crews at ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to leave their vessels immediately.
“In light of the atrocities of the American terrorist army in targeting several tankers of the Islamic Republic of Iran, we warn all tanker crews in the Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports, which host these terrorists and are partners in their atrocities, to immediately leave their vessels, whether at anchor or at the ports, because they will be targeted,” the IRGC Navy said in a statement, according to Iran’s state broadcaster, the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB).
The latest developments mark a sharp escalation in the confrontation between the US and Iran, raising fresh concerns over the security of commercial shipping and energy supplies across the Gulf region.

sources.text:
US Announces What It Has Done To Iran After Attack On Navy Ships, "No American Soldier Was Harmed"
- US Central Command said it struck five Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and near Kharg Island after ballistic missile attacks on US Navy warships
- Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned Iran would keep losing tankers every time it targeted American naval ships
- Brent crude oil prices briefly climbed to $99.46 a barrel as the conflict threatened a key global energy route
PAY ATTENTION: Mark Legit.ng as a preferred source, and our content will appear higher in your Google feed!
The United States military has destroyed five Iranian oil tankers in two separate strike operations, following what American commanders described as repeated ballistic missile attacks by Iran's Revolutionary Guards on US Navy vessels in the region.
US Central Command confirmed on Tuesday, September 4, that the tankers Kivik, Charminar, Horizon 1, and Riesco were hit in the Gulf of Oman, while a fifth vessel, the Derya, was struck near Kharg Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
The military said crews aboard all five ships were ordered to abandon them before the strikes were carried out. No American personnel were harmed during the Iranian missile attacks, which a US warship successfully evaded on two separate occasions over 48 hours.
Iranian state television confirmed the attacks, reporting that tankers were hit near the southern port of Jask and in the Kharg Island anchorage area, and that crew members had been evacuated.
Rubio warns of more strikes to come
Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, September 8, during a visit to Colombia, Secretary of State Marco Rubio made clear the US intended to continue its response.
"Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships. And for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers. And I think you'll see that again today," he said.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Navy escalated the situation further by warning crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels, saying those ships could be targeted in retaliation. The Guards accused both Kuwait and Bahrain of hosting US forces and assisting in the strikes on Iranian tankers.
Hormuz conflict rattles global oil markets
The broader standoff centres on control of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the conflict began.
The US has been escorting a limited number of ships along a route off Oman, while Iran has announced plans to declare its own "exclusion zone" near the strait and insists vessels follow a route of its choosing.
Iran has also introduced a blockade of Iranian ports, limiting the country's oil exports and squeezing its economy. The disruption has pushed Brent crude oil prices to briefly touch $99.46 a barrel on Tuesday, adding political pressure on President Donald Trump and the Republican Party ahead of November's midterm elections.
Danny Citrinowicz, an Iran expert at Israel's Institute for National Security Studies, cautioned against the cycle of strikes and counter-strikes.
"There is no kinetic solution to the Strait of Hormuz problem," he wrote on social media. "Every attempt to impose one only brings Washington and Tehran closer to an escalation that may become increasingly difficult to control."
Saudi Arabia reacts as Houthis rebel attack
Previously, Legit.ng reported that Saudi Arabia accused Yemen's Houthi rebels of striking civilian and economic targets across four of its southern provinces, wounding at least 73 people, among them women and children.
Major-General Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said in a statement that the Houthi attacks hit sites in the provinces of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan and Najran.

sources.text:
US Destroys Five Iranian Tankers After Missile Attacks; Iran Hits Jordan Base as Oil Tops $100
U.S. and Iran Engage in Intense Naval Conflict, Impacting Global Oil Prices
DUBAI — The United States said it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday after ballistic missiles targeted a Navy warship, and Iran answered by firing on a U.S.-used air base in Jordan and claiming strikes on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, the sharpest burst of tanker warfare in a conflict now more than six months old.
U.S. Central Command said the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps twice tried to hit an American warship over two days. "The U.S. warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed," the command said. It identified the tankers as the Kaviz (also rendered Kivik), Charminar, Horizon 1 and Riesco in the Gulf of Oman, and the Derya near Kharg Island, Iran's main oil export hub. Crews were told to leave before the ships were struck and "rendered inoperable," CENTCOM said. It released video it said showed the Riesco burning and sinking. The vessels, it said, belonged to a "multi-billion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, traveling in Colombia, stated the new rule in one sentence. "Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers," he told reporters.
The Guards said they answered with a "heavy missile strike" on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base near Azraq, Jordan, a facility used by U.S. forces. Jordan's armed forces said 20 ballistic missiles were fired from Iranian territory. Eighteen were intercepted. Two fell in unpopulated areas. There were no casualties, Jordan said. A U.S. official said the Jordan strikes were ineffective and that all American troops were accounted for. Iran claimed hangars and shelters were wrecked. That claim was not independently confirmed.
The IRGC also said it hit two U.S. vessels — in some statements naming destroyers — eight oil tankers and 10 ships it called "non-compliant" for entering a zone it has declared off-limits in the strait. It claimed "great damage." CENTCOM did not immediately confirm those hits. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center said several merchant ships in the northern Arabian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman had taken "disabling fire," and that one tanker reported a nearby vessel listing, possibly after a projectile strike.
The exchange follows a similar weekend round. On Saturday, CENTCOM said it struck three Iranian crude carriers after missiles were fired at two U.S. warships, including an aircraft carrier and a destroyer that "evaded" the attack. Iran said it then targeted commercial and U.S.-linked ships. Washington has now made tanker-for-tanker an announced policy: fire at a U.S. combatant, lose export hulls.
Oil moved with the smoke. Brent, the global benchmark, traded through $100 a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since late July before easing. About one-fifth of the world's seaborne oil used to pass Hormuz. Since the war opened with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, the waterway has been mined, restricted, escorted and fought over. The United States says it is enforcing a blockade of Iranian ports and escorting some commercial traffic. Tehran says it will widen an exclusion zone from near Chabahar into the approaches of the strait and put violators on its own sanctions list, according to officials including Mohsen Rezaei.
The White House is running a dual track: sink shadow-fleet tankers and cut what remains of Iran's civilian aviation and trade. The administration announced sanctions on 36 targets, including dozens of Iranian airlines, as the ships burned. President Donald Trump has said repeatedly that Iran will not be allowed a nuclear weapon. He has also tried at times to describe the fighting as contained even as energy prices rise into a U.S. midterm year.
Other fronts moved the same week. Houthi forces in Yemen struck targets in southern Saudi Arabia, wounding scores and setting energy sites alight, according to regional reports, widening a war that already includes Israel and Hezbollah. Neighboring mediators have floated temporary shipping corridors and mine-clearance talks. Those ideas have not stopped missiles on Jordan or hulls in the Gulf of Oman.
What can be stated from official accounts is narrow and grim. The United States says it warned crews off five tankers and destroyed them after two failed shots at a warship. Jordan says it knocked down most of a 20-missile salvo and that no one died. Iran says it hit U.S. ships and a larger group of tankers and will keep closing water. Independent confirmation of how many commercial hulls were actually holed on Wednesday is incomplete. UKMTO's "several vessels" and CENTCOM's video of one Iranian tanker sinking are the firmest public images.
Hormuz is not a metaphor. It is a pinch point where insurance rates, tanker routing and election-year gasoline prices meet anti-ship missiles. A war that both capitals have at times called limited is now eating the ships that pay for it. Rubio's formula — shoot at the Navy, lose a tanker — is simple. So is Iran's: close the gate and fire at the bases that keep it open. Neither formula lowers the price of a barrel once the next hull is on fire.

sources.text:
Iran says its forces have attacked two US vessels and eight oil tankers in the Persian Gulf in retaliation for American strikes on Iranian shipping, marking a further escalation in the maritime conflict gripping the region.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday that the attacks caused “significant damage” and claimed another ten vessels were targeted after allegedly attempting, with US military assistance, to enter an area of the Strait of Hormuz that Tehran has declared unsafe and restricted. The claims have not been independently verified, and Washington has not immediately confirmed damage to US vessels.
The strikes followed an “urgent warning” from the IRGC Navy on Tuesday night instructing crews aboard tankers near ports and anchorages in Bahrain and Kuwait to leave their vessels. “We warn all crew members of the tankers in the vicinity of the docks of Kuwait and Bahrain… to immediately leave their vessels, whether at anchor or at the docks, as they will be targeted,” the command said. Tehran accused Bahrain and Kuwait of facilitating US military operations against Iranian shipping.
Footage subsequently circulated online appearing to show ballistic missiles being launched from several locations in Iran towards US military facilities across the region. Videos reportedly recorded in Jordan also showed heavy air-defence activity, with Patriot systems appearing to intercept incoming projectiles. Open-source intelligence accounts identified Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, east of Amman and used by US forces, as a possible major target, although reports of missile impacts and claims concerning the types of warheads involved have not been officially confirmed.
The latest Iranian action followed US strikes against Iranian oil shipping. US Central Command said American forces destroyed five Iranian crude carriers after the IRGC allegedly twice launched ballistic missiles at a US Navy warship during the preceding two days. According to CENTCOM, four tankers were attacked in the Gulf of Oman and another near Kharg Island, with crews ordered to abandon the vessels before they were disabled.
 
 
Those operations came after an earlier round of US attacks on Saturday, when CENTCOM said three Iranian crude carriers were struck following missile launches towards a US aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer. Two vessels were reportedly disabled, while a third, said to be carrying no oil, was destroyed after its crew evacuated. Iran later claimed retaliatory attacks against three tankers using what Tehran described as an unauthorised route through the Strait of Hormuz, along with three US-linked vessels elsewhere.
The increasingly intense maritime confrontation has emerged as a major front in the six-month conflict. Washington is maintaining a naval blockade restricting shipping to and from Iranian ports, while Tehran has imposed controls of its own over passage through the Strait of Hormuz and announced plans for another restricted maritime zone in the Persian Gulf. The economic stakes are considerable: before the conflict, roughly one-fifth of global oil supplies passed through Hormuz. Growing fears of disruption have pushed energy prices higher, with Brent crude approaching $100 a barrel and US benchmark West Texas Intermediate above $93 on Tuesday.

sources.news_title: U.S. Destroys 5 IRGC Tankers After Iran Targets Another American Warship - Energy News Beat
sources.text:
U.S. Central Command forces destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers on September 8 after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched ballistic missiles at a U.S. Navy warship twice in two days. The American vessel evaded both attacks and continued patrols with no personnel harmed.
CENTCOM identified the targeted vessels as the M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1, and M/T Riesco in the Gulf of Oman, along with the M/T Derya near Kharg Island. U.S. forces directed crews to abandon ship before striking the tankers and rendering them inoperable. The command described the ships as part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network funding the IRGC and its regional proxies, noting Iran has no means to defend them.
The September 8 strikes followed a similar operation three days earlier. On September 5, after IRGC ballistic missiles targeted a U.S. aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer, CENTCOM permanently disabled the M/T Downy off Kharg Island and the M/T Stark 1 near Jask while completely destroying the unladen M/T Kylo (also known as Noxen) in the Gulf of Oman. CENTCOM later confirmed the Kylo sank. Combined, the two operations took eight Iranian-linked tankers out of service.
These kinetic actions mark an escalation from earlier blockade enforcement. The United States first imposed a naval blockade on vessels entering or leaving Iranian ports on April 13, 2026. After a brief lifting under a June memorandum of understanding, the blockade was reinstated on July 14. As of September 7, CENTCOM reported redirecting 94 commercial vessels, disabling three that failed to comply, and boarding two others since the July restart. Earlier in the year, U.S. aircraft used Hellfire missiles, precision munitions, and cannon fire to disable multiple non-compliant tankers attempting to reach Iranian ports, including the M/T Hasna, Sea Star III, Sevda, Lexie, Marivex, Settebello, and Jalveer.
The latest tanker strikes come as Iranian oil exports have collapsed under the blockade. Tracker United Against Nuclear Iran reported that August 2026 saw only three small handymax tankers depart the Gulf of Oman carrying 1.54 million barrels of LPG, with zero crude oil vessels successfully crossing the blockade line. Pre-war monthly exports typically averaged around 55 million barrels. No laden crude tanker has successfully departed the Gulf of Oman since July 12. As of September 8, UANI identified at least 51 tankers laden with Iranian oil clustered along the Iranian coastline, with only 29 loadings recorded since the July 14 blockade restart—just six of them from Kharg Island.
Other trackers corroborate the drop. Vortexa and Kpler estimated Iran loaded 220,000–260,000 barrels per day of crude and condensate in August, down from roughly 740,000 bpd in July and about 2 million bpd in March. June had seen a rebound to 1.75 million bpd after the temporary lifting of restrictions, with UANI tracking 52.7 million barrels that month. July exports fell to about 30 million barrels, or 967,000 bpd. Iran has relied on existing floating storage and ship-to-ship transfers in Asian waters, but those inventories cannot be replenished while the blockade holds.
The repeated targeting of Iran’s limited oil tanker fleet, combined with the ongoing blockade, has sharply reduced Tehran’s primary source of foreign-currency revenue at a time of heightened regional tension. CENTCOM has framed the tanker strikes as a direct economic response to attacks on U.S. naval forces, stating that all IRGC attempts against American warships have failed.

Tehran: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed attacking two US vessels and eight oil tankers in the Persian Gulf in retaliation to a US attack on five Iranian tankers, Iranian state media reported on Wednesday.
In a statement published by its official news outlet Sepah News, the IRGC said that its navy struck the vessels and inflicted heavy damage in retaliation to the “terrorist US Army’s aggression and malicious act of attacking five Iranian oil tankers in the Persian Gulf” on Tuesday night.
It stressed that its naval forces also targeted 10 “violating” ships that sought to cross a “prohibited and unsafe zone” in the Strait of Hormuz with the US Army’s support and provocation.
The IRGC underlined that its navy is exercising complete management and control over the Strait of Hormuz.

Jordan’s military said that its air defence systems have destroyed 18 of 20 Iranian ballistic missiles. Two missiles fell in unpopulated areas, causing no casualties, it said.

“The US warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed,” it added.

The IRGC issued an evacuation warning to the crews of oil tankers at piers in Kuwait and Bahrain following US attacks on Iranian oil tankers off the country’s southern coast on Tuesday night, according to Iranian media.

sources.text:

The Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose 2.1% past the milestone on Wednesday, after conflict increased in the Gulf amid the latest tit-for-tat exchange between Iran and the United States.
The US has attacked several Iranian tankers, while Iran retaliated targeting US navy warship with ballistic missiles, and the US-linked facilities in the gulf countries including gas and oil infrastructure. Supporting Iran, Yemen’s Houthis have also intensified their attack after Saudi targeted the militia recently.
Recently, Houthis attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia, wounding more than 70 people and setting oil installations ablaze. The recent attacks on oil tankers lead to fewer ship-to-ship transfers taking place in the Gulf of Oman will have key role in providing oil to global markets and keeping a lid on prices.

sources.news_title: US sinks Iranian tanker; Iran fires missiles at air base in Jordan
Iran retaliates after US strikes on oil tankers
sources.text:
Iran retaliates after US strikes on oil tankers
The IRGC claims that “significant damage” was done to two US vessels and eight tankers in the Persian Gulf
Iranian forces have struck two US vessels and eight oil tankers in the Persian Gulf in retaliation for attacks on Iranian shipping, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday. It added that the strikes inflicted “significant damage” on the vessels.
The IRGC said it also targeted ten other ships that allegedly attempted, with US military support, to pass through an area of the Strait of Hormuz that Tehran declared prohibited and unsafe. The IRGC said it remains in control of shipping through the strategic waterway. The claims have not been independently verified, and there has been no immediate US confirmation of damage to the vessels.
The attacks came after the IRGC Navy issued an “urgent warning” late Tuesday, telling tanker crews around the docks and anchorages of Bahrain and Kuwait to immediately abandon their ships.
“We warn all crew members of the tankers in the vicinity of the docks of Kuwait and Bahrain... to immediately leave their vessels, whether at anchor or at the docks, as they will be targeted,” the IRGC Navy Command said.
Iranian retaliation began shortly afterward, with numerous videos circulating online showing ballistic missiles being launched from locations across Iran toward US military facilities in the region.

sources.news_title: US Destroys Five Iranian Oil Tankers as Iran Strikes Back at American Forces in Jordan
sources.text:
The military confrontation between the United States and Iran has entered another dangerous phase after U.S. forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers, followed by Iranian missile attacks targeting American positions in Jordan. The latest exchange has intensified fears that the conflict could spread further across the Middle East, while concerns over oil supplies and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz continue to grow.
According to the U.S. military, American forces destroyed five Iranian crude-oil carriers on September 8 after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched missile attacks against a U.S. Navy warship. U.S. officials described the tanker strikes as a response to what Washington characterized as repeated Iranian attacks against American naval forces.
The action represents a significant escalation because the confrontation has moved beyond attacks involving military installations and warships and directly into Iran’s oil-export network. Washington has argued that some of the vessels targeted were connected to networks that help finance Iran’s Revolutionary Guard and its regional military activities.
Iran responded by intensifying attacks against American interests. Iranian forces launched ballistic missiles toward U.S. targets in Jordan, according to reports. Jordanian authorities said most of the missiles were intercepted and reported no casualties from the attack. U.S. officials also assessed that the Iranian strikes had failed to cause significant damage.
The developments are particularly significant because Jordan has been an important location for American military operations in the region. Any sustained Iranian attacks against U.S. forces there could create pressure on Washington to expand its military response.
At the same time, the Strait of Hormuz has become one of the most sensitive areas in the confrontation. Iran’s Revolutionary Guard has warned vessels operating near the waterway and has claimed that it attacked American vessels and commercial ships that entered what it described as a prohibited or unsafe zone.
The waterway is strategically important because a major share of global oil shipments passes through or near the Strait of Hormuz. Any prolonged disruption could affect energy prices far beyond the Middle East.
The economic impact is already becoming visible. Brent crude prices moved above $100 a barrel as traders reacted to the latest escalation and fears over the security of oil supplies.
The latest confrontation therefore has two dimensions: a direct military struggle between Washington and Tehran and a wider economic battle over energy exports. The United States is attempting to restrict Iran’s ability to generate revenue from oil, while Iran is seeking to increase the cost of maintaining U.S. military operations in the region.
The danger now is that every retaliatory action could trigger another response. The destruction of oil tankers was followed by Iranian missile attacks, and any further strikes against U.S. ships or bases could result in additional American military action.
With military forces operating around the Gulf, Jordan and the Strait of Hormuz, the possibility of a broader regional conflict remains a major concern. For global markets, the central question is whether the latest escalation remains limited or develops into a prolonged confrontation that threatens one of the world’s most important energy corridors.
