sources.news_title: Iran Attacks 10 Ships as US Vows More Strikes
sources.text:
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said Wednesday it had attacked two US vessels, eight oil tankers and 10 other ships attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz.
The IRGC said the vessels were trying to enter what it described as a “restricted and unsafe area” of the strait.
The US Central Command (CENTCOM) said it had destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers allegedly linked to a covert network worth billions of dollars that finances the IRGC and its regional proxies.
CENTCOM said the strikes were carried out in response to two failed ballistic missile attacks by the IRGC against a US warship over two days. No US personnel were injured.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that Washington would continue targeting Iranian oil tankers, saying further attempts to attack US vessels would result in additional strikes.
Iran, meanwhile, claimed it had hit two US destroyers equipped with cruise missiles and the Aegis combat system, alleging that both sustained significant damage.
Iranian state television also reported that US forces attacked a commercial vessel off the coast of Jask and targeted two Iranian oil tankers, whose crews were taken ashore.
The escalation follows an Iranian claim that its forces had seized a US unmanned underwater vehicle near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz.
CENTCOM denied that the vehicle had been seized, saying it suffered a technical malfunction more than a day earlier while conducting a maritime surveillance mission.
The US company Anduril confirmed that one of its Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicles had been lost, but said the system was designed to operate in hazardous environments where the loss of a vehicle is possible.
The developments come amid rapidly escalating tensions between Washington and Tehran around the Strait of Hormuz, raising risks to maritime traffic and regional oil supplies.
Source: AFP

sources.news_title: IRGC Says Iranian Missiles Struck Two Aegis-Equipped US Warships, Causing Heavy Damage
sources.text:
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has claimed that its forces carried out ballistic missile strikes against two US Navy destroyers, alleging that the attacks caused significant damage to both vessels.
The claim was reported by Iranian state media in a statement attributed to the IRGC’s aerospace forces.
DDG-119 and DDG-53 Identified as Targets
According to the IRGC statement, the two ships targeted were DDG-119 and DDG-53, both described by Iranian authorities as warships equipped with Aegis air-defense systems and cruise missiles.
The IRGC said the strikes were conducted as part of a military operation, but the statement did not provide details on the number of missiles launched, the location of the attack or the circumstances surrounding the alleged impact.
Iran Claims Significant Damage
Iranian authorities said the ballistic missile strikes inflicted significant damage on the two destroyers.
However, the claim has not been independently verified, and the information provided by the IRGC did not include evidence detailing the extent of the alleged damage or whether there were casualties aboard the vessels.
There was also no immediate independent confirmation of the reported strikes from US authorities in the information cited by TASS.
Claim Raises Stakes in US-Iran Confrontation
If confirmed, a successful ballistic missile attack causing substantial damage to two US Navy destroyers would represent a major escalation in direct military confrontation between Washington and Tehran.
The Aegis-equipped vessels are designed to detect and respond to a range of aerial and missile threats, making the IRGC’s claim particularly significant.
For now, however, the reported attack remains an Iranian military claim pending confirmation from US officials or independent sources.

sources.news_title: Brent Crude Breaks Above $100 as US-Iran Tanker Strikes and Houthi Attacks Escalate
sources.text:
Brent crude broke back above $100 a barrel after US strikes on Iranian tankers and Houthi attacks on Saudi sites turned a tense oil market into a rate problem.
Oil moved first, and everything else had to catch up. Brent touched just over $100 a barrel in early trading on Wednesday, its highest level since July, after a burst of attacks pulled the Strait of Hormuz, Saudi oil infrastructure and the Federal Reserve into the same market conversation. That's the level that matters. If you'd priced in easier money this fall, this is the number that gets in your way.
Five tankers, then Saudi Arabia
The latest jump came after the US military said it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers following missile attacks on a US Navy warship. Five ships, gone. AP reported that the vessels included the Kivik, Charminar, Horizon 1, Riesco and Derya, and that crews were told to evacuate before the strikes. The Financial Times also reported that Iran responded with missile strikes on the Al-Azraq air base in Jordan.
That was enough to move crude. Then the Houthis widened the map.
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement hit Saudi Arabia's southern cities of Khamis Mushait, Abha, Najran and Jazan with drones and missiles on Tuesday. Al Jazeera reported that Saudi-led coalition spokesman Major-General Turki al-Maliki said 73 civilians were wounded, including women and children, and that the attacks targeted civilian and economic sites. A separate Saudi Energy Ministry statement, cited by Al Jazeera, said strikes triggered fires at oil installations and utility sites.
Copper hit a record $14,697 a ton on the LME this week as tariff fears and AI data center demand collide, while Brent crude neared $98 amid renewed US-Iran strikes. Both moves mean the AI buildout just got more expensive to run. - copper hits record high AI data centers - why copper prices rising AI infrastructure boom
Six months into a wider US-Iran conflict, that isn't a stray headline. It's the market's core risk.
The Fed problem is back
Brent had already been climbing before the tanker strikes. Reuters reported in late July that Oman had presented Iran with a Gulf-backed plan to manage the Strait of Hormuz, including voluntary fees for ships using the waterway, while a US official rejected any tolls or restrictions on what Washington says is an international waterway. The strait carries roughly a fifth of the world's oil. You don't need much imagination to see why traders dislike uncertainty there.
The price action matters because inflation was already uncomfortable. The Bureau of Economic Analysis said the PCE price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, rose 3.7% from a year earlier in both June and July, up from 2.9% in December. The Fed's target is still 2%. A fresh oil shock doesn't guarantee another inflation wave, but it makes the clean rate-cut story harder to sell.
Christopher Waller tried to cool that fear last week. Reuters reported that the Fed governor said he would support holding rates steady at the September 15 and 16 meeting if incoming inflation data kept moving toward the Fed's goal. CNBC reported that markets took the remarks as a pause signal, pulling rate-hike odds back toward a coin flip.
Here's the thing: a coin flip is not comfort. It is uncertainty with a price attached.
Energy costs also hit the AI trade in a way investors sometimes prefer to ignore. Chip fabrication, server manufacturing and data center construction all depend on power-hungry supply chains. Higher oil doesn't automatically stop Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft or Meta from building, but it can raise construction costs, lift bond yields and make long-duration growth stocks look less forgiving. Rich valuations need cheap patience. Oil above $100 makes patience more expensive.
The sharper point is that the Fed can't set rates in a vacuum. A central bank can look through a temporary oil move, but it can't pretend Gulf shipping, Saudi energy sites and US-Iran retaliation are just background noise if the move lasts. Traders know that. So do companies planning power contracts and debt issuance for the next wave of data centers.
Brent crude jumped roughly 5% to near $95 a barrel after the US struck Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz following attacks on two oil tankers, reigniting a six-month-old war. The 10-year Treasury yield hit its highest level since 2023 as traders weighed a fresh oil shock against already stretched AI stock valuations. - oil prices spike after US strikes Iran Hormuz - crude oil jumps five percent Middle East tensions
Whether $100 holds now depends less on Wall Street's forecasts than on the next move in the Gulf. Iran gave no sign it was done after the Jordan strike. The Houthis have not said their Saudi attacks are finished. Until that changes, oil is no longer just an energy story. It's sitting inside the rates trade.

sources.news_title: Iran launched ballistic missile barrage targeting U.S. bases in Jordan during the night
sources.text:
AMMAN / TEHRAN — In a major escalation of Middle East tensions, Iran launched a barrage of over 20 ballistic missiles targeting key military installations housing U.S. forces in Jordan during the overnight hours of September 8–9, according to open-source intelligence reports.
The strikes specifically targeted the Al-Azraq Air Base and Muwaffaq Salti Air Base. Military sources indicate that several of the incoming Iranian ballistic missiles were equipped with cluster munition warheads designed to maximize area damage.
Air Defenses Engaged
Jordanian air defense systems actively engaged the incoming barrage, deploying dozens of Patriot surface-to-air interceptors. Jordanian military authorities claim to have successfully intercepted at least 18 of the ballistic missiles.
The strikes appeared intended for maintenance hangars housing high-value aircraft, including U.S. and allied F-35, F-16, and F-15 fighter jets stationed at the facilities.
Strategic Context and Escalation Risk
Tehran claimed responsibility for the strike, framing it as a direct retaliation for U.S. military actions in the Strait of Hormuz on September 8, when American forces struck several Iranian oil tankers following prolonged maritime confrontation.
Casualty figures and the exact extent of structural damage at the airbases remain unverified, with officials maintaining operational security over the impact sites. Defense analysts anticipate an immediate military response from Washington targeting Iranian assets along the critical maritime choke point in the Strait of Hormuz.

sources.news_title: US Sinks Iranian Tanker as Tehran Fires Missiles at Jordan Base
sources.text:
Washington (GNP): The United States military struck five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday, sinking one of them, after Iran twice attempted to target a US Navy warship in the Gulf region. US Central Command said the tankers, linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, were hit in the Gulf of Oman and near Kharg Island. This terminal handles roughly 90 percent of Iran’s crude oil exports.
Tehran responded within hours by launching a barrage of ballistic missiles at a US military base in Jordan. Jordanian authorities said their air defence systems intercepted 18 of the 20 missiles fired, with the remaining two landing in unpopulated areas and causing no casualties. The exchange marks the latest escalation in a confrontation between Washington and Tehran that has intensified over the past week and follows joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran carried out in February.
Central Command confirmed that the American warship evaded both Iranian missile attempts and that no US personnel were harmed in the incident. Officials said the tanker strikes were carried out in direct response to those attempted attacks and described the vessels as part of a shadow fleet funding the Revolutionary Guard and its regional proxies. One of the ships, identified as the M/T Riesco, sank in the Gulf of Oman following the strike.
The Revolutionary Guard’s navy said afterward that it had targeted two American vessels, eight oil tankers and ten other ships attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian state media. The claims had not been independently verified as of Wednesday. The escalation has rattled energy markets, with Brent crude climbing 1.5 percent to trade near 99 dollars a barrel in Asian trading, while US benchmark crude rose 1.3 percent to above 94 dollars.

Compounding the regional instability, Yemen’s Houthi movement launched a drone and missile attack on energy facilities and civilian infrastructure inside Saudi Arabia on the same day, injuring 73 people and forcing a temporary halt to operations at several oil installations, Saudi authorities said.
The latest strikes came hours after Iran’s navy claimed to have seized an unscrewed US submarine drone in the Strait of Hormuz. A Central Command spokesperson said the vessel had malfunctioned more than a day earlier while surveying regional waters and carried no classified sonar, radar equipment, or sensitive data.

sources.news_title: Iran escalates war, strikes U.S. base in Jordan & targets ships near Hormuz
sources.text:
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard says it attacked 10 vessels after the U.S. destroyed five Iranian oil tankers, while Jordan says it intercepted most of the Iranian missiles fired at a U.S.-used military base.
CAIRO/WASHINGTON: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said Wednesday it launched ballistic missiles at a military base in Jordan used by U.S. forces and attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz, sharply escalating the six-month-old conflict.
The strikes came after the United States said it had destroyed five Iranian oil tankers in attacks that Washington described as retaliation for Iranian attempts to strike a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran was continuing to target American naval assets and warned that further attacks would result in additional Iranian tankers being destroyed.
Iran subsequently fired missiles toward a U.S.-used base near Al Azraq in Jordan. The IRGC claimed the attack caused heavy damage, but Jordan said its air defences intercepted 18 of the 20 missiles, while the remaining two landed in unpopulated areas. Jordan reported no casualties.
A U.S. official also said the Iranian attack was ineffective and that all American personnel at the base were accounted for.
Tensions rise around Strait of Hormuz
The IRGC separately claimed it attacked 10 vessels, including two U.S. ships and eight oil tankers, as they attempted to cross what Iran described as a “prohibited and unsafe” area of the Strait of Hormuz.
The strategically vital waterway has already seen a dramatic reduction in shipping traffic following repeated Iranian attacks, raising concerns over global energy supplies.
Iran has also warned oil tankers at ports in Kuwait and Bahrain. A maritime security source said an LNG tanker was damaged at the Emirati port of Khor Fakkan, although responsibility for the incident remained unclear.
Houthis add to regional pressure
The escalation comes as Iran-aligned Houthi forces in Yemen have intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia. Tuesday’s attacks reportedly wounded 73 people and set oil facilities ablaze, adding further pressure to regional energy supplies.
The combined attacks on military targets, shipping routes and energy infrastructure have shattered a month of relative calm and increased fears that the conflict could spread across the region.
Oil approaches $100
Oil prices rose further in early Wednesday trading as markets reacted to the growing threat to tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude moved toward $100 a barrel, reflecting fears that prolonged disruption could tighten global oil supplies.
With U.S. and Iranian forces now striking military and energy-linked targets while regional allies become increasingly involved, the latest exchange marks one of the sharpest escalations of the war in recent months.

The IRGC said the strike targeted maintenance sites, preparation areas, and aircraft hangars used by U.S. forces at the base, deploying a mix of solid- and liquid-fueled ballistic missiles. Iranian state media framed the attack as retaliation for the destruction of the tankers, which CENTCOM said were struck after the IRGC twice targeted a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles over the preceding two days. CENTCOM said the warship evaded those attacks and that no American personnel were harmed in that incident.
As of Tuesday evening, there had been no immediate confirmation from Jordan of damage or casualties resulting from the strike on Al Azraq, and CENTCOM had not issued a public statement addressing the base attack specifically.
Unverified reports began circulating hours after the strike suggesting American casualties. The Hormuz Report, an account tracking the conflict, cited NAYA News, which in turn cited a Jordanian source speaking to Al-Arabiya, in reporting that a large number of U.S. soldiers had been injured, including several with life-threatening wounds, and that the wounded were being transported to Ramstein Air Base in Germany for treatment. The report explicitly noted that the United States had not confirmed either the casualties or any medical evacuations.
Ramstein has served as the main evacuation hub for American service members wounded in the broader Iran war, which began in February 2026 and has produced hundreds of U.S. casualties across bases in Jordan, Kuwait, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia. In previous incidents at Al Azraq, including a July 17 strike that killed three American service members, CENTCOM has typically released official casualty figures within a day, sometimes revising the count upward as more injuries were identified.
No such figures had been released for Tuesday’s strike as of this report. Given the single-sourcing of the casualty claims and the lack of confirmation from CENTCOM, the Pentagon, or Jordanian officials, the scale of any American injuries from the attack remains unverified.
This is a developing story.

sources.news_title: Hormuz tanker war spirals
sources.text:
The maritime war around the Strait of Hormuz has escalated dramatically over the past 24 hours, with the US attacking five Iran-linked tankers and Tehran claiming to have subsequently targeted two US vessels, eight oil tankers and another 10 ships attempting to pass through the strait.
US Central Command said it struck the five tankers on Tuesday after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps twice attempted to hit a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles over the preceding two days.
Four ships – the aframaxes Kaviz and Riesco, product tanker Charminar and LPG carrier Horizon 1 – were attacked in the Gulf of Oman. The Iranian-flagged NITC VLCC Derya was struck near Kharg Island.
US forces instructed crews to abandon the vessels before attacking.
Shipping has become a deliberate instrument of geopolitical leverage
CENTCOM described all five as destroyed, although imagery suggests several were disabled with strikes around their sterns and engine rooms. The 106,500 dwt Riesco was hit more heavily and subsequently sank.
The latest operation means US forces have targeted eight Iranian or Iran-linked tankers within days, following strikes on three vessels over the weekend.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio made clear that Washington intends to continue the policy.
“Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and every time they try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” he said.
Tehran responded on Wednesday with another sharp escalation. The IRGC claimed it had targeted two US vessels, eight oil tankers and 10 other “non-compliant vessels” attempting to cross what Iran calls the prohibited and unsafe area of Hormuz. The claims have not been independently verified.
Iran has also issued an extraordinary warning to crews aboard tankers in Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports to abandon their ships, saying vessels both alongside and at anchor could be targeted because the two Gulf states host US forces.
Damien Chevalier, director of the Maritime Safety Division at the International Maritime Organization, warned that the dangers for shipping extends far beyond Hormuz.
“Shipping has become a deliberate instrument of geopolitical leverage,” he said in an interview with UN News, pointing to attacks in the Black Sea and Red Sea and the resurgence of Somali piracy.
The Consultative Shipping Group of 18 leading maritime nations issued a similar warning this week, arguing international rules underpinning global shipping are being eroded, threatening to fragment both maritime markets and global trade.

This military action was a direct response to repeated attempts by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to strike a US Navy warship using ballistic missiles. These attacks involved the use of ballistic missiles aimed at disrupting American naval operations in the regional waters. However, the US military reported that both attempts were unsuccessful. The American warship managed to successfully evade the incoming missiles and maintained its operational status, continuing its activities in the regional waters without interruption. CENTCOM further confirmed that no American personnel were injured or killed during these hostile attempts by the Iranian forces.
Destruction of Five Iranian Tankers
In response to the failed missile strikes, the US military targeted five oil tankers allegedly linked to the IRGC's oil smuggling network. The operation took place in strategic locations, including the Gulf of Oman and near Iran's Kharg Island. The vessels identified and targeted in the Gulf of Oman were M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1, and M/T Riesco. On top of that, the tanker M/T Derya was targeted near Kharg Island. The US military stated that these vessels were part of a sophisticated network used to transport oil illegally to fund the IRGC and its regional proxies.
Safety Protocols and Evacuation
Before initiating the strikes on the tankers, the US military issued orders for the crews of the targeted vessels to evacuate. This measure was taken to prevent loss of life while ensuring the destruction of the assets. Following the evacuation, the tankers were damaged to such an extent that they were rendered completely inoperable. CENTCOM emphasized that the US warship continued its patrol in regional waters after successfully avoiding the Iranian attacks, and the destruction of the tankers serves as a clear message regarding the protection of American assets and personnel.

CENTCOM has leveled serious allegations against Iran, claiming that these oil tankers are integral components of a secret oil network worth billions of dollars. That previous action was also a retaliatory measure following an Iranian attempt to attack a US aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer. The US military maintains that all recent Iranian attempts to strike US Navy warships have ended in failure, demonstrating the effectiveness of American naval defenses.

Iranian state media has confirmed that two of their oil tankers were targeted in the recent US strikes, specifically mentioning locations near Jask and Kharg Island. The reports from Tehran stated that the crews were safely evacuated and no casualties were reported on their side. In the wake of these attacks, Iran has reportedly issued threats of retaliation against oil tankers operating near the ports of Kuwait and Bahrain, raising concerns about the safety of commercial shipping in the Persian Gulf.

Iran hit back by firing ballistic missiles at Jordan. Iranian state TV, citing the Revolutionary Guard Corps, told tanker crews near Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports to abandon their vessels right away.
This wasn’t an isolated flashpoint. Iran-backed Houthi militants had already struck energy facilities in southern Saudi Arabia days earlier, knocking some sites offline.
The region has been escalating for roughly a week now, and whatever calm existed in oil markets before that is gone.

Some crude is still getting through, but a growing share is on tankers running with their transponders switched off to dodge attacks. China is adding pressure from a different angle.
A pickup in its buying has tightened the market further and lifted prices on select crude grades, a shift from recent months when refiners simply drew down inventories instead of importing more.
India is feeling this harder than most. It leans heavily on Hormuz-linked oil, and its crude basket has already pushed past $106 a barrel, well above where Brent sits.
Other regional grades show the same strain: Murban near $111, Mars above $112, Dubai spot around $105.
As of the latest check, Brent was at $99.70 a barrel and WTI at $94.63, both sharply higher as the US and Iran keep trading strikes with no sign of easing.

sources.news_title: Iran Fires Missiles at US Positions in Jordan After Tanker Strikes Near Kharg Island, Jask
sources.text:
Iran has escalated its confrontation with the United States by launching a missile barrage against US military positions in Jordan, according to Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, citing Arab media reports.
The reported missile attack came after a series of strikes on Iranian maritime assets near Kharg Island and Jask, with Tehran presenting the operation as retaliation for attacks on its oil tankers.
IRIB reported that Iranian missiles were launched towards what it described as enemy positions and claimed that an American military base operating in Jordan was successfully hit. The reports could not be independently verified from the information provided.
Iran Responds After Reported Attacks on Oil Tankers
According to IRIB, an Iranian oil tanker came under attack near the anchorage around Kharg Island. The crew members were reportedly evacuated safely following the incident.
A further strike was then reported against a commercial vessel in waters off Jask County. Another explosion of unidentified origin was also reported in the area, adding to the uncertainty surrounding the sequence of incidents.
The developments have sharply increased tensions around some of the region’s most strategically important maritime routes, particularly the waters surrounding the Strait of Hormuz.
IRGC Issues Warning to Tankers in Bahrain and Kuwait
Following the reported attacks, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy issued a warning to crews aboard tankers located at ports in Bahrain and Kuwait.
The Iranian force accused the United States of attacking Iranian tankers and warned vessels in the two Gulf states to leave their ships immediately.
“In light of the atrocities of the American terrorist army in targeting several tankers of the Islamic Republic of Iran, we warn all tanker crews in the Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports, which host these terrorists and are partners in their atrocities, to immediately leave their vessels, whether at anchor or at the ports, because they will be targeted,” the IRGC Navy said, according to IRIB.
The warning raises concerns about the potential expansion of the conflict beyond direct US-Iranian military targets and into commercial shipping routes.
Iran Claims Capture of US Underwater Drone
The latest missile strikes follow another major claim from Tehran.
Earlier on Tuesday, Iran’s IRGC Navy said it had intercepted and captured a US unmanned underwater vehicle near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz during what it described as an intelligence and operational mission.
According to IRIB, Iranian forces “trapped one of the most modern, intelligent, unmanned submarines” operated by the US military.
Iranian state news agency IRNA said the underwater vehicle contained advanced technology and had been delivered to the US fleet in 2025. Tehran reportedly described the seizure as a “war trophy” and said images of the captured system would be released.
The US side had not independently confirmed the Iranian claim in the material provided.

The escalation comes as US President Donald Trump has continued to speak publicly about the economic consequences of the conflict.
Trump said oil prices would fall sharply after what he described as a US victory over Iran. He also predicted that petrol prices could eventually fall below $2 per gallon.
“Oil prices will drop precipitously, like everything else is dropping (but more!), when we WIN the war with Iran,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Trump also reiterated his position that Iran would not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.
“It will all happen quickly, and Iran will never have a Nuclear Weapon. MAGA!” he wrote.
With Iran now reporting missile strikes against US positions in Jordan, warnings to Gulf shipping and the alleged seizure of a US underwater vehicle, the latest developments indicate a significant escalation in the confrontation and raise fresh concerns over the security of regional waterways and global energy supplies.

sources.news_title: US-Iran War Oil Prices: Brent Hits $99 as Middle East Escalation Drives Energy Market Surge 09-09-2026

US-Iran War Oil Prices Surge Near $100: Market Dynamics and Economic Fallout
Global energy markets are experiencing intense volatility as escalating military clashes between the United States and Iran drive benchmark crude prices to multi-month highs. Brent crude is currently trading near $99 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) has crossed $94 per barrel. US-Iran War Oil Prices
The price surge reflects deep market concern over physical disruptions across Middle Eastern export routes, primarily the Strait of Hormuz. With military exchanges intensifying, targeted tanker strikes, and attacks reported near regional energy infrastructure, the geopolitical risk premium embedded in every barrel of crude has expanded rapidly.
Escalation along Key Maritime Corridors
The primary driver behind the crude rally is the direct threat to energy transit routes in the Persian Gulf. Recent military operations involving US forces and Iranian naval assets have escalated into targeted maritime interdictions and vessel strikes.
- 
Tanker Strikes: Direct exchanges involving commercial tankers and military forces have prompted shipping lines to alter vessel routes or pause transits through the Gulf entirely.
- 
Regional Infrastructure Risks: Collateral threats to regional processing facilities and storage terminals—including recent attacks on energy hubs in the region—have forced insurance underwriters to sharply increase war-risk premiums for oil carriers.
- 
The Hormuz Bottleneck: Roughly one-fifth of global petroleum liquids consumption passes through the Strait of Hormuz. Even partial or temporary bottlenecks create immediate deficits in spot supply markets.  US-Iran War Oil Prices
These developments have widened the spread between global Brent crude and domestic US WTI. Because European and Asian importers rely more heavily on Middle Eastern crude shipments, Brent carries a steeper risk premium than domestic US supply.
Market Buffers and Supply Realities
While prices approach key psychological thresholds, global inventory mechanisms are attempting to cushion the shock. However, structural limits on non-Gulf production mean these buffers can only buy limited time if disruptions persist.
Strategic Reserves and Commercial Stocks
Major consuming nations have begun tapping strategic stockpiles to stabilize domestic fuel supplies. The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) has drawn down significantly alongside commercial holdings in Asia. While reserve releases help cushion initial price spikes, continuous inventory drawdowns leave global markets more vulnerable to sustained supply shocks.
Spare Capacity Constraints
Outside of the immediate conflict zone, major producers hold limited immediate spare capacity. Logistical delays and shipping constraints prevent non-Gulf production from rapidly replacing lost volume in Asian and European import markets. Consequently, global inventories face steady drawdowns.  US-Iran War Oil Prices
Macroeconomic Impact and Inflation Outlook
The surge in energy costs complicates global monetary policy and economic forecasts. Energy prices directly influence transport, manufacturing, and consumer baseline costs, creating persistent inflationary pressure.
- 
Central Bank Dilemma: Persistent elevated crude prices restrict central banks’ flexibility to cut interest rates. If fuel-driven inflation accelerates, monetary authorities may hold benchmark interest rates higher for longer, weighing on broader economic growth.
- 
Refinement and Fuel Spreads: High raw crude costs flow into refined product markets, driving up prices for diesel, gasoline, and jet fuel. This increases supply chain costs across global freight networks.
- 
Consumer Demand Destruction: If Brent crude maintains levels above $100 per barrel, sustained high retail fuel prices could trigger demand destruction, reducing broader consumer spending across non-essential economic sectors.  US-Iran War Oil Prices
Energy Market Scenarios
The trajectory of crude prices over coming quarters hinges on military developments and maritime security along main transit routes. Market analyst projections focus on two primary potential paths:
Scenario A: Sustained Escalation (Brent > $105/bbl)
If military operations directly disrupt physical processing hubs or lead to a sustained blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, real supply shortfalls will replace risk premiums. Under this scenario, emergency inventory releases will fail to offset volume losses, pushing crude toward multi-year highs.
Scenario B: Maritime De-escalation (Brent $80–$85/bbl)
If diplomatic channels establish protected transit corridors or military actions de-escalate, the geopolitical risk premium built into current pricing will unwind. Prices would then re-align with baseline global supply and demand fundamentals.  US-Iran War Oil Prices
Until maritime safety through key energy corridors is restored, global energy markets will remain highly sensitive to real-time security developments in the region.

The organization urged ships operating in the area to monitor the latest maritime security information and remain alert to the rapidly changing operational environment.
Tensions rise around strategic waterway
The incidents mark a sharp escalation in military activity involving Iran, the United States and regional states, particularly around the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global oil shipments.
The latest developments come despite a memorandum signed in June that envisioned an agreement to reopen the strategic waterway as part of a broader effort toward a peace deal.

It said it has no reports of casualties. Jordan is a staunch US ally that hosts American forces, making the kingdom’s military bases a target of repeated Iranian strikes. US Central Command said it had no information to offer.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US will not allow Iran’s attacks to go unanswered.

The US military also destroyed the vessel Derya, which was located near Kharg Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The statement said the crews of the five vessels were told to abandon ship before the attacks.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy on Tuesday had warned crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels, saying the ships could be targeted in retaliation for US attacks on Iranian tankers. It accused Kuwait and Bahrain of hosting US forces and assisting in the attacks.
A US blockade of Iranian ports has squeezed the country’s economy by limiting its oil exports, while the American military has been helping a limited number of ships transit on a route through the Strait of Hormuz off Oman. Tehran wants ships to follow a route that it chooses through the strait, which was considered an international waterway before the war.

sources.news_title: US Destroys 5 Iranian Tankers as Iran Retaliates
sources.text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Sept. 9, 2026 (STL.News) The United States military destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers, including one near strategically important Kharg Island, after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps allegedly attempted to strike a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles, triggering another significant escalation in the six-month conflict between Washington and Tehran.
Iran responded by launching ballistic missiles toward a military base in Jordan used by U.S. forces and claimed attacks against 10 vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian state media and international reporting.
The rapidly developing confrontation has once again placed one of the world’s most important energy corridors at the center of the conflict while pushing oil prices toward $100 per barrel and further disrupting commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
U.S. Central Command said American forces destroyed five Iranian crude carriers Tuesday after the IRGC attempted to strike a U.S. Navy warship twice with ballistic missiles during the preceding two days.
The Navy vessel successfully evaded the attempted attacks, according to CENTCOM, and no American personnel were reported injured.
U.S. forces targeted five tankers: the M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1, M/T Riesco, and M/T Derya.
Four were struck in the Gulf of Oman. The Derya was struck near Kharg Island, home to Iran’s most important oil export terminal.
CENTCOM said crews aboard the vessels were directed to abandon ship before the American attacks.
US Strike Reaches Waters Near Kharg Island
The Derya’s location makes the latest operation particularly significant.
Kharg Island sits in the Persian Gulf off Iran’s southwestern coast and has historically played a central role in the country’s petroleum export system. The U.S. attack therefore occurred near one of Iran’s most strategically important energy locations.
However, the distinction between attacking a vessel near Kharg Island and attacking the island’s infrastructure is important.
Current reporting indicates that the Sept. 8 American strike targeted the Derya near Kharg Island, rather than representing a newly announced U.S. attack against Kharg Island’s oil facilities.
U.S. officials have described the targeted tankers as part of a network used to generate revenue for the IRGC and Iranian-backed groups throughout the Middle East.
The latest attacks came only three days after another American operation against Iranian oil carriers.
On Sept. 5, CENTCOM announced that U.S. forces had struck three Iranian crude oil carriers after the IRGC launched ballistic missiles toward a U.S. aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer.
CENTCOM said both American warships successfully evaded those attacks and no U.S. personnel were injured.
In that operation, American forces permanently disabled the M/T Downy off Kharg Island and the M/T Stark 1 near Jask, while completely destroying the M/T Kylo, also known as the Noxen, in the Gulf of Oman.
CENTCOM characterized those ships as part of a multibillion-dollar network supporting the IRGC and its regional proxies.
The Sept. 8 operation therefore represents a substantial expansion of the U.S. campaign against Iran’s maritime oil network.
Iran Retaliates Against US Forces
Iran responded quickly.
The Revolutionary Guard said Wednesday that it fired ballistic missiles at a military installation near Al Azraq, Jordan, used by American forces.
Iran claimed the attack caused heavy damage, but those claims have not been independently verified.
Jordan provided a significantly different account.
Jordanian authorities said air defenses intercepted 18 of 20 Iranian missiles, while the remaining two fell in unpopulated areas. No casualties were reported.
A U.S. official described the Iranian attack as ineffective and said American personnel were accounted for.
The conflicting accounts underscore the importance of distinguishing between independently confirmed developments and wartime claims issued by the governments and military organizations involved.
Iran also claimed Wednesday that its forces attacked 10 ships, including two American vessels and eight oil tankers.
The Revolutionary Guard alleged that the vessels were attempting to cross what Iran described as a prohibited and unsafe section of the Strait of Hormuz.
The extent of the damage claimed by Iran was not immediately independently confirmed.
However, maritime authorities have reported additional incidents involving commercial vessels in the region, demonstrating the increasingly dangerous conditions facing shipping operators.
Strait of Hormuz Traffic Plunges
The escalating military confrontation carries implications extending far beyond Iran and the United States.
The Strait of Hormuz is one of the most important energy transportation corridors on Earth.
Before the current war began on Feb. 28, approximately 125 large commercial vessels typically moved through the strait each day, according to shipping data cited by Reuters.
The route historically handled approximately 20% of the world’s daily crude oil and liquefied natural gas supply.
Traffic has since fallen dramatically.
Preliminary Kpler shipping data showed only six commodity vessels crossed the Strait of Hormuz Tuesday, compared with nine Monday and a 10-day average of approximately 12.
Five of Tuesday’s vessels entered the waterway, and only one exited.
The figures do not include vessels that may have turned off their Automatic Identification System transponders to reduce their visibility.
The declining traffic illustrates how dramatically the conflict has altered commercial activity around the Persian Gulf.
Washington has attempted to maintain limited maritime movement while simultaneously restricting Iranian petroleum exports. Tehran, meanwhile, has sought to exert greater control over vessels moving through the strategic waterway.
The result is an increasingly dangerous contest involving naval forces, commercial tankers and some of the world’s most important energy infrastructure.
Oil Prices Approach $100
Energy markets are responding accordingly.
Brent crude approached $100 per barrel early Wednesday, reaching its highest level since July as traders weighed the possibility of further disruptions to Middle Eastern oil production and transportation.
Brent has risen roughly 25% since early August as hopes for a lasting resolution to the conflict diminished and military activity intensified.
West Texas Intermediate crude also moved higher.
The significance extends beyond oil traders and energy companies.
Sustained increases in crude prices can eventually translate into higher gasoline, diesel, aviation, and transportation costs. Those increases can filter through supply chains and place renewed upward pressure on consumer prices.
The possibility of prolonged disruption around Hormuz matters because alternative transportation routes cannot easily replace all the petroleum historically moving through the strait.
Markets are therefore watching both the military confrontation and commercial shipping data closely.
Regional Conflict Expands
The renewed U.S.-Iran confrontation is unfolding alongside additional instability across the Middle East.
Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen launched attacks against several Saudi Arabian cities Tuesday, including strikes involving drones and missiles.
Saudi authorities reported dozens of people wounded and fires at oil-related facilities.
The attacks further complicated efforts to maintain stable energy supplies while increasing the possibility that additional U.S. allies could become more deeply involved in the regional conflict.
The Houthis have also historically threatened maritime traffic around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another crucial shipping corridor connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
The simultaneous instability surrounding Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb creates an unusually serious threat to maritime trade because the two waterways serve as critical routes for oil, natural gas, and international commerce.
US and Iran Enter Another Dangerous Phase
The latest exchange represents a sharp reversal after approximately a month of relative calm.
The broader war began Feb. 28 with joint U.S.-Israeli attacks against Iran and has since developed into a combination of military confrontation and economic pressure.
Washington has sought to weaken Tehran’s ability to finance military operations and allied groups by restricting Iranian petroleum exports.
Iran has responded by threatening American military assets, U.S. allies, and maritime traffic.
The destruction of five Iranian tankers Tuesday demonstrates that the United States is increasingly willing to impose direct economic costs when Iran targets American warships.
Iran’s subsequent missile attack toward the U.S.-used base in Jordan demonstrates that Tehran remains willing to retaliate.
That cycle creates an obvious escalation risk.
An unsuccessful missile attack can produce a retaliatory strike. That strike can generate another response, potentially creating increasingly destructive rounds of military action even when neither side initially intends a much broader confrontation.
The commercial consequences are already visible.
Tankers have been destroyed or disabled. Commercial shipping has declined sharply. Oil prices have approached or exceeded psychologically important levels, and countries across the region face increased security risks.
Kharg Island Remains Critical
Kharg Island will remain one of the locations to watch closely as the confrontation develops.
The island’s importance to Iran’s petroleum industry makes military activity around it especially consequential.
For now, the latest verified U.S. action near Kharg Island involved the destruction of the M/T Derya, rather than a newly announced attack against the island’s petroleum infrastructure itself.
That distinction could become critical if the conflict continues to escalate.
Direct attacks against major Iranian petroleum infrastructure could have substantially different economic and military consequences than attacks against individual vessels.
The situation remained fluid early Wednesday, Sept. 9, as governments, maritime authorities and military officials continued assessing the overnight attacks.
Additional U.S. or Iranian military action could quickly change conditions throughout the Persian Gulf.
For global markets, meanwhile, attention remains focused on whether commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz can continue and whether crude oil supplies from the region will face additional disruption.
With five Iranian tankers destroyed Tuesday, Iran retaliating against U.S. interests and commercial traffic through one of the world’s most important energy corridors severely reduced, the confrontation between Washington and Tehran has entered another dangerous phase.
Editor’s note: This is a developing story. Military claims from the United States, Iran and other governments may change as additional information becomes available. STL.News distinguishes between independently confirmed information and claims made by parties involved in the conflict.

CENTCOM said US forces instructed the tanker crews to abandon the vessels before carrying out strikes that rendered the ships inoperable. No casualties among the crews were reported.
The US command described the tankers as crude oil carriers operated by the IRGC and alleged that they were part of a multibillion-dollar network used to finance the Iranian military organisation and its regional proxies.
CENTCOM did not identify the US warship that Iran allegedly targeted, disclose the locations of the attempted attacks or say how many ballistic missiles were fired.
The latest action came four days after another US operation against Iranian oil carriers. On September 5, CENTCOM said US forces destroyed three Iranian crude oil tankers after the IRGC allegedly attempted to attack a US aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer.
Kharg Island, located in the Persian Gulf, has historically been a key terminal for Iran’s seaborne crude oil exports. The escalation of military activity around the island has raised concerns over commercial shipping and energy supplies in the region.
A prolonged disruption to shipping could increase tanker insurance and freight costs and put upward pressure on global crude prices, potentially affecting major oil importers such as India.

US Strikes Five Iranian Oil Tankers After Attacks
US-Iran Tensions Escalate as Tanker Strikes Trigger Retaliatory Threats
TEHRAN: (News Desk) – US forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday after Iran launched two ballistic-missile attacks against a US Navy warship in recent days, further escalating the confrontation between Washington and Tehran.
US Central Command said the crews of all five tankers were ordered to evacuate before American forces struck the vessels and rendered them inoperable. The military described the operation as a response to what it called Iran’s latest failed attacks on US naval assets.
According to Central Command, an American warship successfully evaded two separate missile attacks by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps over a two-day period and continued its patrols in regional waters.
The latest strikes came only days after US forces destroyed three Iranian crude carriers on Saturday. Washington said those attacks followed unsuccessful Iranian attempts to target a US aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer.
Iran has warned that attacks on its oil tankers would trigger retaliation against US bases and commercial vessels associated with American allies in the Gulf. Iran’s armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi said Tehran would target US positions across the region if Washington continued striking Iranian tankers.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the American campaign, saying Washington would continue targeting Iranian oil carriers whenever Tehran attempts to strike US naval vessels.
The confrontation widened further on Wednesday when Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed they had attacked two US vessels, eight oil tankers and 10 other ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian authorities said the vessels had ignored warnings to leave an area declared unsafe and restricted.
Iran also threatened to target oil tankers operating near Kuwait and Bahrain, two key US allies in the Gulf, in retaliation for the American strikes.
Later, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed responsibility for a missile attack on the US Al-Azraq air base in Jordan. Iranian state media reported damage to maintenance facilities, aircraft deployment areas and fighter-jet shelters. Jordan’s military, however, said it intercepted 18 missiles launched from Iran toward its territory.
The escalating exchange of attacks comes amid growing restrictions on maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical global route for oil and gas shipments. Washington is also intensifying efforts to restrict Iran’s ports and increase economic pressure on Tehran.
Iran claims capture of US underwater drone
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has also claimed that it captured an American unmanned underwater vessel operating in the Strait of Hormuz and released images that it said showed the operation.
US Central Command disputed the Iranian account, saying the underwater vessel experienced a technical malfunction while conducting patrol operations in the strait in support of US Navy activities.
CENTCOM said the craft was an older model that did not gather sensitive intelligence and was not fitted with classified radar or sensor equipment.
The conflicting claims highlight the rapidly deteriorating security situation in the Strait of Hormuz, where American and Iranian forces are conducting military operations amid heightened regional tensions.

Oil prices rose above the crucial $100 level for the first time since July on Wednesday, up for a fourth straight session as the US-Iran conflict flared over control of the Strait of Hormuz.
International benchmark Brent crude futures were up 2.1 percent at just over $100 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate crude rose 1.7 percent to $94.63. Brent has gained around a quarter since early August as the war in the Middle East intensified.
Five Iranian crude oil carriers were destroyed on Tuesday after Tehran targeted a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days, US Central Command said.
“The US warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed,” Centcom said in a social media post, adding that the vessel M/T Riesco sank in the Gulf of Oman following the US strike.

“Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” Rubio said.

Gulf stock markets ended in positive territory on Tuesday.
Dubai’s main share index rose 0.3 percent, while Abu Dhabi gained 0.5 percent. Saudi Arabia’s benchmark index ended 0.1 percent higher.

sources.text:

US forces destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers in the Middle East noting them as retaliatory strikes after IRGC targeted an American Navy warship
Washington: US Central Command (CENTCOM) said that its forces destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers in the Middle East on Tuesday, noting them as retaliatory strikes after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted an American Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over a 48-hour period.
According to a statement by CENTCOM, the targeted American warship successfully evaded both attempted missile strikes and suffered no personnel injuries or operational damage, remaining on active patrol in regional waters.
“U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) forces destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers, Sept. 8, after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days. The U.S. warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed,” the statement read.
CENTCOM stated that in response to the attempted attacks by Iran, US forces conducted coordinated strikes against five vessels belonging to Iran’s state-linked maritime fleet. Four crude oil carriers, the M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1, and M/T Riesco, were destroyed in the Gulf of Oman, while a fifth vessel, the M/T Derya, was hit near Kharg Island.
It added that US forces issued direct instructions commanding the crews of all five vessels to evacuate prior to the strikes
“In response to Iran’s most recent failed attacks, CENTCOM destroyed the IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1, and M/T Riesco in the Gulf of Oman as well as M/T Derya near Kharg Island. American forces directed the crews to abandon ship before the vessels were struck and rendered inoperable,” CENTCOM stated.
The US military command emphasised that the targeted fleet operates as a primary financial mechanism for Tehran’s security apparatus, identifying the vessels as “part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies.”
“Iran has no means by which to defend these vessels,” it stated.
Tuesday’s action marks the second major operation against Iranian maritime infrastructure within three days.
“On Sept. 5, CENTCOM forces destroyed three Iranian crude oil carriers after the IRGC tried to attack a U.S. aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer. All IRGC attempts against U.S. Navy warships have failed,” CENTCOM noted.
On the other hand, Iran’s IRGC launched ballistic missile strikes against a US military airbase in Jordan and two American Navy destroyers, according to state media reports.
In an official statement carried by Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB), the IRGC stated that the military operation, codenamed “Ya Haidar Karrar”, was launched to avenge recent US attacks on Iranian oil tankers.
The IRGC confirmed that its forces targeted the US-operated Al-Azraq airbase in Jordan using liquid- and solid-fuel ballistic missiles. According to the statement, the strikes hit aircraft hangars and shelters housing F-35, F-16, and F-15 fighter jets.
“In response to the aggressive actions and evil harassment of Iranian oil tankers and ships by the terrorist army of the Great Satan, the powerful aerospace force of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps… attacked the DDG-119 and DDG-53 combat destroyers carrying cruise and Aegis missiles with powerful ballistic missiles,” the IRGC statement read.
“As a result of this attack, significant damage was caused to these vessels,” it added.
The IRGC added that its military operations will continue until all US attacks against Iranian shipping cease, warning Washington against any further actions in regional waters.
“The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and other armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran continue to declare their firm determination to respond to the desperate actions of the US regime and warn the enemy against any miscalculation,” the statement added.
Regional air defences were activated across neighbouring countries as the missiles crossed regional airspace.
According to Al Jazeera, Jordanian air defence units intercepted at least eight Iranian missiles over Amman and other cities.
Al Jazeera also reported that multiple types of missiles were spotted near the Jordanian-Syrian border, while Syrian state television reported that Syria intercepted incoming Iranian missiles over the border city of Irbid.
Earlier in the day, Iran’s IRGC Navy claimed that its forces had captured a US unmanned submersible at the entrance of the Strait of Hormuz during a complex intelligence and operational operation.
According to IRIB, the IRGC Navy said the submersible was equipped with the latest technology in the underwater field and was delivered to the US fleet in 2025.

sources.news_title: US Strikes Iranian Tankers After Tehran Targets American Military Bases
sources.text:
Missiles, drones and oil tankers have become the latest flashpoints in a widening Middle East war, after Iranian-backed Houthis struck several Saudi cities, the US military hit multiple Iranian crude carriers and Iran said it launched ballistic missiles at a US base in Jordan.
The Houthis targeted four cities in southern Saudi Arabia, injuring 73 people and igniting fires at oil-related sites in what appeared to be a significant escalation in the six-month-old conflict.
With traders weighing the risk of disrupted supplies, the US military’s Central Command announced it had destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers and released video of the strikes. CENTCOM said the action followed two alleged attempts by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to hit a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles over the previous two days.
No Americans were harmed, the US said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington would keep responding militarily to Iranian attacks.
“Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” Mr Rubio told reporters during a visit to Colombia.
Iranian missiles are intercepted by Jordanian air defense systems above Damascus in Syria
Iran then struck back, saying it carried out a ballistic missile attack on a US base near Al Azraq town in eastern Jordan, according to an IRGC statement carried by state media.
Iranian state media published video it said showed missiles being launched toward Jordan.
Iran claimed the salvo caused heavy damage. Jordan, however, said its air defences intercepted 18 of the 20 missiles, with the remaining two falling in unpopulated areas, and reported no casualties.
Iran has repeatedly hit US allies across the region during the war, including several strikes on Jordan, one of which killed two Us military personnel in July.
In a separate statement, the IRGC also said it attacked two US destroyers, according to state media.
The US military had yet to respond to the reports.
Iran also threatened to target oil tankers in Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports, according to a statement carried by state media.
A maritime security source reported that a liquefied natural gas tanker was damaged in the Emirati port of Khor Fakkan, though responsibility was unclear.
Brent crude oil remained below $100 per barrel, despite the disruptions
After a quieter August, the US and Iran resumed exchanging fire in recent days, pushing benchmark Brent crude to its highest level since 23 July 23.
Even so, prices stayed below $100 (€85) per barrel despite the disruptions.
The conflict has repeatedly moved in fits and starts, with pauses giving way to flare-ups. Iran has continued to launch missile and drone strikes on neighbours and threaten oil shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, even as US attacks have degraded much of its conventional forces and deepened the strain on its already troubled economy.
The Houthis — who control most of Yemen’s populated areas, including the capital — have also ratcheted up pressure on US allies by intermittently disrupting shipping at the entrance to the Red Sea on the far side of the Arabian Peninsula.
Yesterday, the Houthis said they carried out a wide operation deep inside Saudi territory, using drones and missiles to hit a Saudi airbase in Khamis Mushait and Saudi state oil company assets in Abha, Najran and Jazan.
NASA satellite images showed a thick plume of black smoke over the Jazan refinery and a column of white smoke rising from an oil distribution centre in Abha.
Saudi authorities reported fires at the locations and said women and children were among the 73 wounded.
Reports of such a high number of injuries suggested the strikes were among the largest against Saudi Arabia since the United States and Israel began their war against Iran in February.
Houthi attacks on southwestern Saudi Arabia have the potential to worsen the war’s global economic impact
At the same time, Iranian tankers came under attack again, signalling a resumption of US strikes on Iran after a two-day pause.
The US said it destroyed four IRGC crude oil carriers in the Gulf of Oman and a fifth near the oil hub of Kharg Island, after Iranian media had reported some of the incidents.
“American forces directed the crews to abandon ship before the vessels were struck and rendered inoperable,” the Central Command statement said.
Houthi strikes in southwestern Saudi Arabia could deepen the war’s global economic impact by threatening Middle East energy flows beyond the already blockaded Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia has led an Arab coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen for more than a decade.
That war had eased in recent years, but a ceasefire has since collapsed.
In recent days, Saudi-backed Yemeni forces aligned with a southern-based government have launched a multipronged offensive into Houthi-held areas after the Houthis tried to push into government-controlled positions.
The government — forced from the capital by the Houthis 12 years ago — said it now intends to retake all territory held by the group.
The broader confrontation in the Gulf has become a contest of resolve between Washington and Tehran, with both sides betting that economic pressure from rival blockades will compel the other to back down.
The US Treasury announced new aviation-related sanctions yesterday, saying the measures were designed to ground Iran’s airlines.
Washington is seeking to keep oil moving to global markets by guiding vessels through the Strait of Hormuz, while simultaneously trying to choke off Iran’s exports with a blockade.
Central Command said the tankers it struck were part of a shadow network used to finance the IRGC and its regional proxies.
Iran has long backed what it calls an “Axis of Resistance”, including Hamas, Lebanon’s Hezbollah, Iraqi Shi’ite militias and the Houthis.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they captured a US submersible near the strait.
A US official said an underwater drone malfunctioned more than a day ago and said it did not carry classified sonar or radar equipment.
CENTCOM spokesperson Captain Tim Hawkins, without saying whether Iran seized the device, said: “An underwater drone operated by US forces malfunctioned more than a day ago.
“It was surveying regional waters in support of ongoing operations.”
He added the “defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment”.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards had said they seized a US underwater drone at the “entrance to the Strait of Hormuz in a complex intelligence and operational action”, describing it as “one of the most modern, unmanned and smart submarines” operated by US forces.

The Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB), citing Arab media, confirmed that a batch of Iranian missiles dived toward enemy targets, with Iranian missiles successfully striking a US base operating in Jordan.
The missile offensive follows a succession of US strikes on Iranian maritime assets in regional waters.
IRIB reported that an initial attack targeted an Iranian oil tanker near the Kharg Island anchorage, where crew members were safely evacuated. Moments later, US forces carried out a subsequent attack on a commercial vessel in the coastal waters off Jask County, alongside another explosion of unidentified origin reported in the area.
In response to the hostilities, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy issued an urgent evacuation warning, according to IRIB.
Addressing the crew of maritime vessels in neighbouring ports, the IRGC vowed to retaliate by targeting oil tankers near Bahraini and Kuwaiti ports.
“In light of the atrocities of the American terrorist army in targeting several tankers of the Islamic Republic of Iran, we warn all tanker crews in the Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports, which host these terrorists and are partners in their atrocities, to immediately leave their vessels, whether at anchor or at the ports, because they will be targeted,” the IRGC Navy declared according to IRIB.
Tensions across the strategic waterways and regional host nations remain at critical levels as both military forces continue exchanging strikes.
Earlier on Tuesday, Iran’s IRGC Navy claimed that its forces had captured a US unmanned submersible at the entrance of the Strait of Hormuz during a complex intelligence and operational operation.
According to IRIB, the IRGC Navy fighters “trapped one of the most modern, intelligent, unmanned submarines” belonging to the US military at dawn.
The IRGC Navy said the submersible is equipped with the latest technology in the underwater field and was delivered to the US fleet in 2025.
According to Iran’s state news agency IRNA, the vessel is equipped with the world’s most advanced underwater technology and has been seized as a “war trophy.”IRNA further reported that photographs of the captured submersible are expected to be released in the coming hours.
The development comes as US President Donald Trump claimed on Monday (local time) that oil prices will drop sharply once the United States achieves victory in its conflict with Iran, forecasting gas prices could fall below two dollars per gallon.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump linked high energy costs directly to ongoing military operations in the Middle East, asserting that post-war markets would stabilise rapidly.
“Oil prices will drop precipitously, like everything else is dropping (but more!), when we WIN the war with Iran,” Trump wrote. “Three Dollars a gallon, but ultimately, below Two Dollars a gallon.”
Trump further reiterated his threat that the US will not let Iran have a nuclear weapon. “It will all happen quickly, and Iran will never have a Nuclear Weapon. MAGA!” he added.
Source: ANI

sources.news_title: Iran claims missile strike on US base in Jordan in retaliation to attacks on oil tankers - Pakistan Observer
Iran strikes US base in Jordan after US attacks Iranian oil tankers
sources.text:
Iran strikes US base in Jordan after US attacks Iranian oil tankers
Iran threatens further action against regional shipping, raising concerns over the Strait of Hormuz and global oil supplies
Iran struck back at the United States on Wednesday, firing a barrage of ballistic missiles at a US military base in Jordan after American forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and near Iran’s Kharg Island.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said its aerospace forces targeted the Al-Azraq Air Base in Jordan in retaliation for what Tehran described as “aggressive” US attacks on Iranian oil tankers. The IRGC said the strike hit a hangar used for the maintenance, repair, preparation and deployment of US F-35, F-16 and F-15 fighter jets, as well as aircraft shelters, claiming to have inflicted “heavy damage” on the base.
Iran’s missile strike marked a direct and forceful response to Washington’s expanding military pressure on Tehran and its efforts to choke off Iranian oil exports. The latest escalation also demonstrated Iran’s willingness to carry the confrontation beyond its immediate borders and target US military infrastructure in the region.
Jordan said its air-defence systems intercepted 18 of the 20 Iranian ballistic missiles fired towards the kingdom. The other two missiles fell in unpopulated areas, with no casualties reported.
The Iranian retaliation followed a major US operation against Iran’s oil trade. US Central Command (CENTCOM) said American forces had destroyed five Iranian crude-oil tankers after the IRGC allegedly attempted twice to strike a US warship with ballistic missiles over the preceding two days.
The vessels — M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1, M/T Riesco and M/T Derya — were attacked in the Gulf of Oman and near Kharg Island, a crucial hub for Iran’s oil exports. US forces said tanker crews were ordered to abandon the vessels before the ships were struck and rendered inoperable.
Washington has described the tankers as part of a multibillion-dollar network allegedly operated by the IRGC to generate revenue for Iran’s military and regional allies. Tehran, however, has framed the US attacks as part of a broader campaign against its economy and sovereignty.
The latest confrontation places Iran’s oil industry and maritime routes at the heart of the escalating conflict. Kharg Island is particularly significant to Tehran because it serves as a major outlet for Iranian crude exports, making attacks in and around the area potentially consequential for the country’s ability to sustain its oil revenues.
Iran has also threatened further action against shipping in the region, raising fresh concerns over the security of vital maritime routes and the Strait of Hormuz, through which a substantial share of the world's oil supply passes.
The confrontation has already rippled through global energy markets, with Brent crude moving towards $100 a barrel as traders weighed the prospect of further disruption to Iranian oil exports and shipping through the Gulf.
For Tehran, Wednesday’s missile barrage was more than a military reprisal: it was a signal that attacks on Iran’s oil lifeline could invite direct retaliation against US forces across the region. As Washington intensifies pressure on Iran’s energy network, the danger of a wider confrontation is mounting, with the Gulf’s oil routes and US military bases increasingly becoming flashpoints in the escalating standoff.
With agency inputs

sources.news_title: US destroys five Iranian tankers after warship targeted with ballistic missiles
sources.text:
US destroys five Iranian tankers after warship targeted with ballistic missiles
text_fields
Washington: The United States has destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and near Kharg Island after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) twice fired ballistic missiles at a US Navy warship, according to US Central Command (CENTCOM).
The command said the American warship evaded both missile attempts over the previous two days and that no US personnel were harmed. In response, US forces struck the tankers on Tuesday, ordering the crews to abandon ship before rendering the vessels inoperable. No casualties were reported among the tanker crews.
CENTCOM identified the destroyed ships as M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1 and M/T Riesco in the Gulf of Oman, and M/T Derya near Kharg Island, a major Iranian oil export terminal in the Persian Gulf. The vessels were described as IRGC-operated crude carriers forming part of a multibillion-dollar network that funds the Guard and its regional proxies.
The US military did not name the warship targeted, specify the location of the missile attempts or say how many missiles were fired. The operation marks the second US strike on Iranian tankers in four days; on 5 September, CENTCOM destroyed three Iranian crude carriers after the IRGC attempted to attack a US aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer.
Kharg Island has long handled a large share of Iran’s seaborne crude exports, and military activity in its vicinity raises concerns over the security of commercial shipping and energy supplies in the Gulf. Analysts warn that any sustained disruption to tanker traffic could push up insurance and freight costs and affect global oil prices, with implications for major importers such as India.
(Inputs from IANS)

sources.news_title: US Military Destroys Five Iranian Tankers Amid Escalating Tensions
sources.text:
The US military reported on 9 September 2026 that it had destroyed five Iranian oil tankers as part of an escalating conflict between the two nations. This action followed alleged Iranian missile attacks aimed at American warships. The ongoing hostilities, which have persisted for over six months, have intensified tensions in the region.
Iranian media claimed that missiles were fired towards US targets in Jordan in retaliation for the recent strikes. Jordan’s military confirmed that its air defence systems intercepted a total of 18 ballistic missiles, with two landing in uninhabited areas. Fortunately, no casualties were reported in these incidents. The strife has raised concerns about security in the region, particularly given Jordan’s position as a key ally of the United States.
The US Central Command, which oversees military operations in the area, stated it could not provide further information regarding the situation. The destruction of the five tankers is part of a broader strategy by the Trump administration to enforce economic and military pressure on Iran.
Iran’s Response to US Actions
The Iranian Revolutionary Guards had reportedly attempted missile strikes against a US aircraft carrier and destroyer shortly before the destruction of the tankers. This led to increased military readiness from the US, with American officials warning they would take measures against what they perceive as threats to their naval assets. According to reports, the tankers destroyed on Tuesday included the Kivik, Charminar, Horizon 1, and Riesco, situated in the Gulf of Oman, alongside the Derya near Kharg Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
In advance of these air strikes, Iranian state media indicated that a new “exclusion zone” would be established near the Strait of Hormuz, aimed at preventing vessels from entering areas deemed risky due to the escalating military activities. This move illustrates Tehran’s intent to assert its influence in the strategically crucial waterway, through which a significant percentage of the global oil supply transits.
As the situation developed, Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a statement affirming the US’s resolve to retaliate against any further threats from Iran. He emphasised that any attacks against US naval vessels would result in a US response, underscoring a commitment to maintain military presence and operational readiness in the region.
Economic Implications and Strategic Concerns
The recent military actions coincide with renewed sanctions imposed by the Trump administration targeting various segments of Iran’s aviation sector, presumably aimed at isolating Tehran economically. With rising energy prices impacting the global market, the Brent crude oil price reached USD 99.46 a barrel on 9 September 2026. This escalation poses challenges not just for the involved nations but also for global economic stability.
Danny Citrinowicz, an expert from Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies, cautioned that ongoing exchanges of military actions could lead to uncontrollable escalation, with adverse effects on the global economy. He observed that attempts to impose military solutions to the complexities of the Strait of Hormuz would likely exacerbate tensions between Washington and Tehran.
The latest developments highlight the precarious nature of the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, both in military and economic terms. With the potential for further conflict, the region remains under close scrutiny from international observers, as the US and Iran navigate their fraught relationship. This ongoing conflict serves as a reminder of the volatile dynamics at play in one of the world’s most critical maritime corridors.
